## E21. Benchmarks that are not calibrated on Gaussian data only

Script `experiments/e21_benchmarks.py`; methods `src/avmonitor/benchmarks_robust.py`; outputs `results/e21_*.csv` and `results/figures/e21_*.png`; tests `tests/test_benchmarks_robust.py`; iteration notes `docs/iterations/E21.md`. Q21a to Q21c are **[SYNTHETIC]**, Q21d is **[REAL]**, and the literature statements are marked **[PUBLISHED]** with what could and could not be checked. Every setting, seed, target and number of paths was fixed before the reported runs (iteration 1 of the notes); the changes made after the first runs are listed in "Post hoc decisions" at the end.

**Question.** The referee (M5) observed that the competitors of E4 and E13 were calibrated on Gaussian data, that BOCPD had a Gaussian observation model, that the "BJV-type" test was reconstructed without the paper (renamed "VR scan" in E13), and that no classical detector on the e-detector's own statistic and no econometric monitoring procedure was tried, so that the benchmarks favour the proposed method. Three questions follow. (i) At the same false alarm rate on clean data, what does Ville's distribution-free threshold cost in delay against a threshold calibrated for the true law? (ii) When the law is not Gaussian, does a threshold calibrated by simulation or by a bootstrap of the calibration window keep its rate? (iii) How do a robust BOCPD and a CUSUM monitoring procedure with a training sample compare, on simulated and on real data?

**Summary.**
* **At equal false alarm rate on Gaussian data, Ville's threshold costs the e-detector's statistic almost nothing.** [SYNTHETIC] With thresholds calibrated by simulation to the e-detector's own first-day rate on clean Gaussian data (1.3%), the same Shiryaev-Roberts betting statistic detects increases of the sd by 25%, 50% and 100% in 106, 41 and 20 steps against the e-detector's 100, 39 and 19, and decreases about 10% faster (144 against 162 steps at × 0.8). A Page CUSUM on the same truncated statistic is as fast for increases and 15% to 40% faster for decreases, where the e-detector's bets are capped by validity (E11). The price of a distribution-free threshold shows only against thresholds that spend the full 5% per day: 1.1 to 1.3 times the delay for increases and 1.4 to 2.1 times for decreases, at 4.5% to 4.9% false alarms per day instead of 1.3%, and only if the law is known.
* **Thresholds calibrated on Gaussian data do not carry over to other laws, even on the truncated statistic; a bootstrap of the calibration window repairs this for i.i.d. laws.** [SYNTHETIC] Gaussian-calibrated CUSUMs on X reach 5.0% to 8.2% per day under Student t3 and t5 (target 1.3%) and 14% to 22% (target 5%); the HKZ-type rule on raw r² reaches 10% to 15% under Student t3 and jumps. Per-path bootstrap thresholds stay at 1.4% to 2.2% (target 1.3%) and 4.9% to 6.3% (target 5%) under all six i.i.d.-type laws. With bootstrap thresholds under Student t3 the e-detector detects increases 16% to 24% faster than the CUSUM, and the CUSUM detects decreases 3% to 10% faster. Under GARCH and slow stochastic volatility every rule alarms on most paths, the e-detector included; the HKZ-type rules, whose long-run variance absorbs part of the clustering, alarm least (21% to 52% in the first day).
* **A Student t BOCPD fixes plain BOCPD's false alarms but not its dependence on the law, and loses small changes.** [SYNTHETIC] On E13's paths BOCPD-t (ν = 3, exact run-length recursion on a variance grid) has 0.7% false alarms per day under jumps and 3.3% under Student t5, against 73.2% and 53.2% for E13's Gaussian BOCPD, but 4.9% under Student t3 and 0.5% under Gaussian data with the same threshold; within 1500 steps it finds only 56% of 25% increases and 77% of 20% decreases (e-detector 98%), while it is faster than the e-detector for halvings of the sd (27 against 81 steps).
* **CUSUM monitoring with a training sample (HKZ-type) is robust only on the truncated statistic and is about twice as slow.** [SYNTHETIC] On X = min(r², τ²) its rate holds under every i.i.d.-type law (1.1% to 1.6% at a 1.3% target); its delays are about twice the e-detector's, because its boundary is of order c σ sqrt(m) (derived below). Asymptotic critical values for open-ended monitoring spend almost none of their 5% in the first day for γ ≤ 0.25.
* **On real data, classical rules on the e-detector's own statistic and design are as precise as the e-detector; BOCPD-t and the HKZ-type rules are not.** [REAL] Matched to the e-detector's numbers of up and down alarms on the five coins (both half-years, bands 0 and 0.25), SR betting with a calibrated threshold and the two CUSUMs on X are never significantly less precise than the e-detector in 24 comparisons of the next-day outcome (differences -5.0 to +3.0 points; one significant difference, in favour of SR betting). The HKZ-type rules are below it in 13 of 16 comparisons (6 significant), BOCPD-t in 20 of 24 (14 significant), although BOCPD-t improves on E13's Gaussian BOCPD. E13's advantage over BOCPD and the VR scan therefore appears to come from the statistic and the design (truncated squared returns against a one-day baseline, recalibrated after each alarm), not from the betting form or from Ville's threshold; what the threshold adds is a false alarm guarantee that needs no calibration and no assumed law.
* **What could not be checked.** [PUBLISHED] The texts of Knoblauch, Jewson and Damoulas (2018), Horváth, Kokoszka and Zhang (2006) and Chu, Stinchcombe and White (1996) could not be opened from this machine. BOCPD-t is therefore not the β-divergence method, and the monitoring rules are "of the type" of HKZ and CSW, with a boundary verified for monitoring in linear models and critical values from simulation.

### The competitors

All rules see the same returns: a calibration window (2000 steps in the simulations, 1440 minutes on real data) and then the monitored stream.

* **Classical rules on the e-detector's statistic.** X_t = min(r_t², τ²) with τ = 3 times the scaled MAD of the calibration window and m0 the mean of X over that window, as for the e-detector; Y_t = X_t / m0. *Page's two-sided CUSUM on Y*: G_t = max(0, G_{t-1} + Y_t - 1 - k) for increases and max(0, G_{t-1} + 1 - Y_t - k) for decreases, with the reference value of the Gaussian likelihood ratio for a change of the variance by a factor θ (k = θ log θ / (θ - 1) - 1 for θ > 1 and k = 1 - θ log θ / (θ - 1) for θ < 1; on untruncated Gaussian returns this is exactly the likelihood-ratio CUSUM): "small" for sd × 1.25 and × 0.8 (k = 0.240 and 0.207) and "medium" for × 1.5 and × 0.67 (k = 0.460 and 0.348). *SR betting*: the e-detector's own Shiryaev-Roberts betting statistics (the same six increase and five decrease bets), with a calibrated threshold in place of the level 2A that Ville's inequality gives. Each side of a two-sided rule gets half of the target rate.
* **Two calibrations.** (a) *Gaussian simulation*: 20,000 clean Gaussian paths, one 390-step day after a 2000-step calibration window; the targets are the e-detector's own first-day rate on the same paths (1.305%, "matched") and 5% (the e-detector's bound for one day, A = 7800). (b) *Bootstrap of the calibration window*, per path: 1000 replicates, each a resampled calibration window (giving m0*) and a resampled 390-step stream of X values, Y* = X* / m0*; each side's threshold is the 1 - α/2 quantile of the replicate maxima. τ is kept (X is already truncated at τ²). This is the calibration a practitioner could run without assuming a law; it assumes i.i.d. returns.
* **BOCPD-t.** Bayesian online change-point detection (Adams and MacKay 2007) with a Student t observation model with ν = 3 fixed (the heaviest Student law with a finite variance) and an unknown variance on a grid (65 values from 0.04 to 25 times the unit variance in the simulations, log step 0.1; 71 values from e^-6 to e^4.5 times a predictable centre on real data, log step 0.15). The prior is E13's inverse gamma prior (α0 = 2, mean equal to the calibration mean square, or on real data the robust variance of the previous day) discretised on the grid; hazard 1 / A; runs of at least w steps are lumped into one class, which is exact for a constant hazard; alarm on the posterior log-odds of a run shorter than w (w = 250 as in E13); direction from the posterior mean variance of the short runs against the lumped class. The filter is the exact run-length recursion for this discrete model (tests: it equals the conjugate Gaussian filter of E13 when the t is replaced by a Gaussian, and the lumped recursion equals the unlumped one). It is calibrated as E13 calibrates BOCPD: threshold matched to the e-detector's rate on E13's own 4000 Gaussian calibration paths (1.55%), and the rule "posterior probability of a short run at least 0.5".
* **HKZ-type monitoring with a training sample.** The calibration window is the training sample of size m. Detector Q(m, k) = sum of Z over the first k monitored steps minus k times the training mean of Z, with Z = r² (the setting of the published procedure) or Z = X (our robust variant), standardised by sqrt(m) times a Bartlett long-run standard deviation of the training Z (bandwidth floor(m^(1/3)) = 12). Alarm when |Q(m, k)| / (σ sqrt(m)) ≥ c (1 + k/m) (k / (m + k))^γ, with γ = 0.25 (primary), 0 and 0.45; the sign gives the direction. A second boundary, sqrt(x (x - 1) (c² + log(x / (x - 1)))) with x = (m + k) / m, is that of OLS-CUSUM monitoring in the R package strucchange ("CSW-type"). Critical values: asymptotic, for open-ended monitoring at 5% (simulated quantile of sup_{0<t<1} |W(t)| / t^γ, 20,000 paths; for the strucchange boundary c solving 2 (1 - Φ(c) + c φ(c)) = 0.05), and calibrated on Gaussian data like the rules above (one critical value for |D|).
* **Reference.** The robust two-sided e-detector with a plug-in baseline, each side alarming at 2A, A = 7800 (1440-minute days and A = 28,800 on real data), computed with per-path decrease bets exactly as `VolatilityMonitor` does (unit test). On E13's paths E13's own version (decrease bets common to a batch) is also run, and reproduces E13's numbers exactly (checked in the script).

**[PUBLISHED] What could be checked.** Web searches on 3 November 2026; arxiv.org, the NeurIPS proceedings site and publisher full texts could not be opened from this machine, and no attempt was made to get around the block.
* Knoblauch, Jewson and Damoulas (2018), "Doubly robust Bayesian inference for non-stationary streaming data with β-divergences", NeurIPS 31: robust BOCPD by general Bayesian inference with β-divergences, robust both for the parameters and for the change-point posterior (proceedings and institutional listings). The equations could not be read, so a β-divergence version could not be built and checked; BOCPD-t is the Student t version that the referee allowed instead, and it is *not* their method.
* Horváth, Kokoszka and Zhang (2006), "Monitoring constancy of variance in conditionally heteroskedastic time series", Econometric Theory 22(3), 373 to 402 (Cambridge Core and RePEc listings): sequential monitoring of the unconditional variance with a training sample, with theory through a strong invariance principle for the squared observations. Their detector and boundary could not be read; we therefore call our rule "HKZ-type". The boundary g(m, k) = c sqrt(m) (1 + k/m) (k / (m + k))^γ, 0 ≤ γ < 1/2, and its limit sup_{0<t<1} |W(t)| / t^γ were verified, through search excerpts, for monitoring in linear models (Horváth, Hušková, Kokoszka and Steinebach 2004, Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference 126(1), 225 to 251; restated in later papers by some of the same authors).
* Chu, Stinchcombe and White (1996), "Monitoring structural change", Econometrica 64(5), 1045 to 1065 (Econometric Society and RePEc listings). Their boundary could not be read in the paper; the "CSW-type" boundary is the one implemented in strucchange (version 1.6-0, `R/monitoring.R`, read from the CRAN mirror on GitHub), which cites later work, so it is a sensitivity check and not a reproduction.

### Q21a. False alarms in the first day [SYNTHETIC]

**Design.** Calibration window of 2000 steps from the same law as the monitored data (so jumps and fat tails are part of "normal"), then 780 monitored steps; 4000 fresh paths per law (seeds 21100 to 21107), the bootstrap rules on the first 2000 of them (1000 replicates per path, seeds 21150 to 21157). Laws as in E13, plus Student t3: Gaussian; Student t3 and t5 (unit variance); jumps (probability 0.005 per step, size N(0, 8²)); price noise (sd 0.5); prices rounded to a tick of 0.5 sd (about 20% zero returns); slow stochastic volatility (log-sd 0.15, half-life 390 steps); GARCH(1, 1) with α = 0.05 and β = 0.94. Under the last two the volatility drifts, so the null of a constant baseline is false by construction and every rule alarms. The table gives the share of paths with an alarm in the first 390-step day (`results/e21_null.csv`, which also has two days and the γ = 0 and 0.45 Gaussian-calibrated rows). Bold: the 95% Wilson interval lies above the rule's calibration target (1.3% or 5%; for the asymptotic rows, 5%), in the first six columns. Wilson half-widths are about 0.4 points at 1.3% and 0.7 points at 5% with 4000 paths, and 0.6 and 1.0 points with 2000.

**Reading.**
* **The e-detector's own statistic with a calibrated threshold behaves like the e-detector.** Matched to the e-detector's Gaussian rate, SR betting has 1.6% under Gaussian data and 1.4% to 2.5% under the other i.i.d.-type laws, against 1.2% to 2.1% for the e-detector itself. With the Gaussian threshold for 5% it has 4.9% under Gaussian data but 6.1% to 7.6% under Student t, price noise and ticks. A threshold calibrated by simulation does not carry over to other laws; Ville's threshold has a guarantee of 5% for all of them (it is not attained, E9 and E16).
* **The Gaussian calibration of a CUSUM fails under fat tails even on the truncated statistic.** CUSUM on X matched to 1.3% reaches 5.0% to 8.2% under Student t3 and t5, and with the 5% threshold 14% to 22%. Truncation removes the effect of single large returns (jumps: 1.9% to 2.2%), but under a Student law the whole distribution of X / m0 changes shape (more small values and more values at the cap), and the CUSUM's threshold depends on that shape.
* **The bootstrap of the calibration window removes most of the dependence on the law.** Bootstrap thresholds keep SR betting at 1.5% to 1.8% and CUSUM small at 1.4% to 2.2% (target 1.3%), and at 5.1% to 6.0% and 4.9% to 6.3% for the 5% target, under all six i.i.d.-type laws. They are slightly above target even for Gaussian data, as expected: each side's threshold is an empirical quantile of 1000 replicates, and if the bootstrap law were the true law, the value that `np.quantile` returns there would have an expected tail probability of 0.75% instead of 0.65% per side at the 1.3% target, and 2.6% instead of 2.5% at 5%. The largest excess is under price noise (6.0% and 6.3% at 5%), whose noise makes successive returns dependent, which an i.i.d. bootstrap ignores. Under slow SV and GARCH the bootstrap rules, like all others, alarm on 46% to 58% and 82% to 90% of paths in the first day.
* **The HKZ-type rule on raw r² fails under fat tails; on X it holds.** With Gaussian critical values the rule on r² has 10.0% (t3) and 11.8% (jumps) against 1.3%, and 12.5% and 14.8% against 5%. Its standardisation by the long-run variance of r² presumes a finite fourth moment of the returns, which Student t3 lacks, and with jumps the squared returns are so skewed that early in monitoring, where the boundary is small, a few large values cross it. On X = min(r², τ²) the same rule stays at 1.1% to 1.6% and 4.7% to 5.1% under all six laws: X is bounded, and its Bartlett standardisation adapts to its law.
* **Asymptotic critical values say little about the first day.** For γ = 0 and 0.25 the open-ended critical value spends almost none of its 5% in the first 390 steps (0.0% to 0.2% under Gaussian data, price noise and ticks, and on X under all six laws), because 390 steps are only k / m = 0.2 of the training sample; for γ = 0.45 and the strucchange boundary the first day takes 2.8% to 5.1% (same laws). The open-ended check (`results/e21_hkz_open_end_check.csv`): over 20,000 steps (10 m) the γ = 0.25 rule on Gaussian r² has 4.6% against 4.3% for the limit over the same range.
* **GARCH: the HKZ-type rules alarm least** (21% to 52% in the first day against 82% to 92% for the betting and CUSUM rules). They compare the monitored mean with the training mean, standardised by a long-run variance that includes the clustering of the training sample, whereas the betting and CUSUM rules scale by m0 alone. Q21b shows what this costs in delay.

### Q21b. Delay in the E4 design [SYNTHETIC]

**Design.** As E4: calibration window of 2000 steps, then 3500 monitored steps with a change of the sd by the stated factor at step 500; 1000 paths per law and factor (seeds 21200 to 21235), the bootstrap rules on the first 500 of them (seeds 21250 to 21285). All rules see the same paths. Cells: median delay in steps from the change to the first alarm after it (share of paths with an alarm after the change); **FA** is the share of paths with an alarm in the 500 steps before the change, shown when it is 5% or more. Thresholds were calibrated for 390 steps, so over these 500 steps the rules matched to 1.3% have 1% to 4% and the 5% rules 4% to 10% under Gaussian data. Full results, with mean delays, the share of detections that point the right way and detection within one day, are in `results/e21_change.csv`.

**Reading.**
* **At the e-detector's own Gaussian rate, a calibrated threshold on the same statistic buys almost nothing.** SR betting with Gaussian-matched thresholds: 106, 41 and 20 steps for increases against the e-detector's 100, 39 and 19, and 144, 92 and 67 for decreases against 162, 102 and 75. The e-detector's increase side uses more than half of its false alarm rate; matching each side at half moves rate from the increase side to the decrease side, which is all the difference. On Gaussian data, Ville's threshold costs this statistic nothing at equal false alarm rate.
* **Classical CUSUMs are faster for decreases.** CUSUM small at the same rate: 106, 41, 19 for increases (as the e-detector) and 138, 68, 45 for decreases (15% to 40% faster); CUSUM medium is faster for large changes (35 and 15 steps at × 1.5 and × 2; 58 and 32 at × 0.67 and × 0.5) and slower for small ones. For decreases the e-detector's bets must be valid for every law with Y ≤ B, which caps them at 1 / (B - 1) (E11); a CUSUM calibrated for one law has no such cap.
* **Spending the full 5% buys 10% to 30% for increases and 40% to 110% for decreases, on Gaussian data only.** With thresholds for 5% per day, SR betting needs 80, 34, 17 and 113, 72, 54 steps and CUSUM small 81, 32, 15 and 105, 54, 36: the e-detector's delays are 1.1 to 1.3 times theirs for increases and 1.4 to 2.1 times for decreases, at a first-day false alarm rate of 1.3% instead of 4.5% to 4.9%. The same Gaussian thresholds give 7.5% (SR betting) and 17.7% (CUSUM small) per day under Student t3 (Q21a), and FA 10% to 24% before the change here.
* **With a law-free calibration the CUSUM's advantage shrinks under fat tails.** Bootstrap thresholds keep the CUSUM's false alarms down under Student t3 (no FA of 5% or more at the matched rate), and its delays then are 240, 79, 38 for increases against the e-detector's 202, 64, 29 (the e-detector 16% to 24% faster), and 258, 104, 63 for decreases against 266, 116, 69 (the CUSUM 3% to 10% faster). Under Student t5 the picture is the same (increases: e-detector faster by 15% to 23%; decreases: bootstrap CUSUM faster by 6% to 19%). Bootstrap SR betting is slower than the e-detector in 10 of the 12 Student t cells, equal in one and faster in one (t5, × 0.8: 194 against 201 steps). Under jumps the rules on X are about as fast as under Gaussian data; under ticks the Gaussian-calibrated CUSUM is too conservative (164 steps at × 1.25 against 118) and its bootstrap version is as fast as the e-detector.
* **The HKZ-type rules are about twice as slow.** On Gaussian data 199, 82, 35 and 330, 204, 140 steps on r² at the matched rate, 284, 122, 61 and 453, 273, 184 on X with the asymptotic critical value. This is a property of the boundary: Q(m, k) is the departure from the training mean accumulated since monitoring began, and the boundary c σ sqrt(m) (1 + k/m) (k / (m + k))^γ is about 104 squared-return units at k = 600 (c = 1.83, σ = sqrt(2) for Gaussian r², m = 2000), so an increase of the variance by 0.5625 per step (sd × 1.25) needs about 185 steps after the change, plus the growth of the boundary meanwhile; Page's CUSUM and the e-detector restart their evidence whenever it turns against a change. On r² under jumps the rule detects only 40% to 88% of changes, with 12% to 13% false alarms before them, and at × 0.8 it points the wrong way in 9% of detections (46% for γ = 0.45). On X it is reliable, but slow.
* All rules on X, with matched or bootstrap thresholds, point the right way in 99.7% to 100% of detections at × 1.25 and × 0.8.

### Q21c. BOCPD-t in E13's design [SYNTHETIC]

**Design.** E13's online design, on the very paths of E13: calibration window 2000, A = 7800, hazard 1 / A, w = 250; null paths of Q13b (1000 per law, seeds 13310 to 13316) and 1000 fresh Student t3 paths (seed 21400); change paths of Q13c (200 per cell, change at step 500 of 2000, seeds 13400 to 13429). BOCPD-t's threshold, matched to the e-detector's 1.55% on E13's 4000 Gaussian calibration paths (seeds 13300, 13301, reproduced exactly), is a short-run log-odds of -0.805 (`results/e21_bocpd_thresholds.csv`). **Reading.**
* **BOCPD-t keeps its false alarms down where BOCPD broke** (jumps: no cell with FA of 5% or more, against 78% to 83%; Student t5: at most 6%, against 58% to 63%) and finds large changes fast: 27 and 64 steps at sd × 0.5 and × 0.67 under Gaussian data, against the e-detector's 81 and 109, and 34 steps at × 2 against 20.
* **The price is power for small changes.** Within 1500 steps it finds 56% of sd × 1.25 changes and 77% of × 0.8 changes under Gaussian data (46% and 80% under jumps, 56% and 78% under t5), against 96% to 99% for the e-detector. This is consistent with what the model assumes: a Student t model with ν = 3 treats large returns as weak evidence about the variance (its Fisher information for log σ per observation is 2ν / (ν + 3) = 1, half the Gaussian value 2), so a 25% change of the sd builds up evidence slowly; if it is not declared within w = 250 steps, the run that started at the change is itself in the long-run class against which the alarm statistic compares, and it may never be declared.
* **The classical rules on X repeat Q21b on these paths**: at the same Gaussian rate CUSUM small is as fast as the e-detector for increases and faster for decreases (140, 66, 45 against 169, 109, 81), and the HKZ-type rule on r² fails under jumps (22% to 87% detected, FA 8% to 13%).

### Q21d. Real data: five coins in E13's design [REAL]

**Design.** E13's real-data design (Q13d) on the five Binance coins (BTC, ETH, XRP, SOL, DOGE): one-minute returns divided by the predictable intraday profile of E6b, 1 July to 31 December 2025 (184 days) and 1 January to 30 June 2025 (181 days, E13's held-out half-year). The e-detector uses its frozen real-data settings (A = 28,800 per 1440-minute day, calibration 1440, c = 3, bands 0 and 0.25); its alarms are E13's, reproduced exactly (checked in the script). The rules on X and the HKZ-type rules run as the e-detector runs: calibrate on 1440 minutes (for the HKZ-type rules, the training sample), monitor, and after an alarm recalibrate on the next 1440 minutes (the restart loop reproduces `VolatilityMonitor` alarm for alarm, unit test). BOCPD-t runs continuously with E13's predictable prior (the robust variance of the previous day) and pauses for 1440 minutes after each alarm, with w = 250 (E13's first run), 720 and 1440 (E13's longer windows); each series is divided by the median of that prior over the 30 days before the monitored period, a constant known in advance, so that one relative grid serves all coins (the filter is scale-equivariant). Thresholds are rate-matched per series to the e-detector's numbers of up and down alarms at band 0 and at band 0.25, as in E13 (this uses the data but not the outcome). Under restarts the alarm counts are not monotone in the thresholds (iteration 2 of the notes), so matching uses a bisection followed by a local and a grid search; the counts reached are in `results/e21_real_h2_matched_thresholds.csv` and `results/e21_real_h1_matched_thresholds.csv`. For reference the rules are also run at Gaussian-matched thresholds for 1440-minute days (E13's 2000 Gaussian paths, seeds 13500 and 13501, at the e-detector's simulated 3.95% per day; `results/e21_real_thresholds.csv`). Validation and tests as in E13: after an up (down) alarm, is the robust volatility of the next day above (below) an EWMA forecast made with past data only; the same at four hours; two-proportion z-test and week-clustered sandwich test against the e-detector at the same band. The bootstrap calibration is not used here: matching the alarm counts replaces any calibration of the threshold.

**Results, band 0.25** (`results/e21_real_pooled.csv`; band 0 is in the same file). Rows marked E13 are copied from `results/e13d_real_long_windows_pooled.csv`, and the e-detector's row is identical in both files (checked). Shares are over the alarms that can be scored, whose number is in brackets. p-values against the e-detector at the same band: two-proportion z-test / week-clustered test (as in E13).

**Reading.**
* **Matched to the e-detector's alarm counts, the classical rules on its own statistic and design are as precise as the e-detector.** Over the eight comparisons per rule (two half-years, two bands, two directions; next-day outcome), SR betting with a calibrated threshold, CUSUM small and CUSUM medium are never significantly below the e-detector (week-clustered p ≥ 0.05 in all 24; differences from -5.0 to +3.0 points, mean -0.8 to -1.6), and SR betting is once significantly above it (Jan to Jun 2025, band 0, down alarms: 69.2% against 66.3%, week-clustered p = 0.019, z-test p = 0.35). This suggests that the e-detector's advantage over BOCPD and the VR scan in E13 comes from what these rules share (truncated squared returns measured against a baseline calibrated on a full day, and recalibration after each alarm), not from the betting form or from Ville's threshold. On the four-hour outcome the three rules are within -9.9 and +5.9 points of the e-detector, with significant differences in both directions (3 below, 2 above, of 24).
* **The HKZ-type rules are less precise**: below the e-detector in 13 of 16 comparisons (on r²: 8 of 8, 3 significant; on X: 5 of 8, 3 significant), by 2.8 (X) and 5.2 (r²) points on average.
* **BOCPD-t improves on E13's Gaussian BOCPD but stays below the e-detector.** At w = 250 (Jul to Dec 2025, band 0.25) it scores 69.0% and 70.7% against E13's 67.8% and 61.7%; with longer windows it comes closer (w = 1440: 69.7% and 77.0% against 78.5% and 80.5%). Over its 24 comparisons it is below the e-detector in 20, significantly in 14 (w = 250: 7 of 8; w = 720: 4; w = 1440: 3). On the four-hour outcome BOCPD-t with w = 250 is at or above the e-detector in all 8 comparisons, and significantly above it for down alarms (70.1% to 78.1% against 60.3% to 67.4%), as E13 found for short windows: such alarms mark changes over hours that need not last a day.
* **Gaussian-matched thresholds.** SR betting raises almost the same numbers of alarms as the e-detector (763 and 757 against 764 and 757), with almost the same precision. The CUSUMs raise 4% to 6% more alarms, with lower precision for down alarms in Jul to Dec 2025 (62.2% and 63.5% against 68.3%, week-clustered p < 0.001 and 0.006) and none in Jan to Jun. The HKZ-type rules raise far fewer alarms at their Gaussian critical values (on r²: 133 and 292; on X: 501 and 522), and with fewer alarms their up alarms are more often followed by a day above the forecast in Jan to Jun 2025 (86.7% and 81.6% against 74.8%, week-clustered p = 0.004 and 0.033; not in Jul to Dec). BOCPD-t at its Gaussian threshold raises 821 and 797 alarms, with lower precision (60.9% and 56.7% in Jul to Dec 2025, p < 0.001).
* **Matching precision.** Per series and band, |up count - target| + |down count - target| is 0 to 4 alarms for the restart rules (mean 0.75) and 0 to 9 for BOCPD-t (mean 1.2; E13's bisection, whose counts are also not monotone because of the pause after each alarm), out of 119 to 154 target alarms per series (`results/e21_real_h2_matched_thresholds.csv`, `results/e21_real_h1_matched_thresholds.csv`). Pooled over the coins, the numbers of scored alarms differ from the e-detector's by at most 8.
* **Multiplicity.** The p-values are not adjusted: this section makes 64 next-day comparisons at matched rates (8 rules, 8 each), so about 3 would fall below 0.05 by chance if no rule differed from the e-detector; 21 do, all but one of them for BOCPD-t and the HKZ-type rules.

### What was not done, and why

* **No β-divergence BOCPD.** Knoblauch, Jewson and Damoulas (2018) could not be read from this machine, and a version "of the type" whose construction we could not check against the paper would not answer the referee. BOCPD-t is a different, simpler robust BOCPD, named as such.
* **No exact HKZ or CSW procedure.** Neither paper could be read. The HKZ-type rule uses the verified boundary of monitoring in linear models applied to squared returns (the setting of HKZ), with critical values from simulation, so it is a procedure of their type and not their procedure; the CSW-type boundary is strucchange's.
* **No bootstrap on real data**, because rate matching sets the thresholds there (Q21d).
* **No block bootstrap.** The i.i.d. bootstrap was the pre-registered calibration; a block bootstrap, which would respect the dependence that price noise creates, was not tried.

### Post hoc decisions

* The count-matching search for the restart rules (iteration 2) was added after a timing run on BTC showed that bisection alone missed the targets by up to 25 alarms; it uses the alarm counts only, not the outcome, and was fixed before any real-data outcome of E21 was computed except in a smoke test of the pipeline on DOGE for two rules (iteration 4 of the notes), after which nothing was changed.
* The real-data Gaussian-matched threshold of BOCPD-t is computed with the real-data grid (decided before any real-data run).
* The rule for bold entries in the tables (95% interval above the target) and the choice of which rows to show were made when writing this section, after the results.
* Everything else (rules, reference values, γ, bandwidth, ν, grids, w, targets, seeds, numbers of paths, laws) was fixed in iteration 1.

### References used in E21

* Adams, R. P. and MacKay, D. J. C. (2007). Bayesian online changepoint detection. arXiv:0710.3742 (as in E13).
* Chu, C.-S. J., Stinchcombe, M. and White, H. (1996). Monitoring structural change. *Econometrica* 64(5), 1045 to 1065. Listing verified; text not read.
* Horváth, L., Hušková, M., Kokoszka, P. and Steinebach, J. (2004). Monitoring changes in linear models. *Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference* 126(1), 225 to 251. Listing verified; boundary and limit verified through search excerpts of later papers on monitoring (for example Aue, Horváth, Kokoszka and Steinebach 2008, *Test* 17, 515 to 530); text not read.
* Horváth, L., Kokoszka, P. and Zhang, A. (2006). Monitoring constancy of variance in conditionally heteroskedastic time series. *Econometric Theory* 22(3), 373 to 402. Listing and abstract verified; text not read.
* Knoblauch, J., Jewson, J. and Damoulas, T. (2018). Doubly robust Bayesian inference for non-stationary streaming data with β-divergences. *Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems* 31. Listing verified; text not read.
* Page, E. S. (1954). Continuous inspection schemes. *Biometrika* 41(1/2), 100 to 115.
* strucchange, R package, version 1.6-0, file `R/monitoring.R` (CRAN mirror on GitHub), read on 3 November 2026.

## E22. E12's FOMC and CPI test with monitors that carry a proved per-day bound

Script `experiments/e22_guaranteed_events.py`; pre-registration `docs/preregistration_e22.md` (commit `949c1d5`, made before any part of E22 was run on real data); outputs `results/e22_*.csv` and `results/figures/e22_release_rates.png`; tests `tests/test_e22.py` [SYNTHETIC]; iteration notes `docs/iterations/E22.md`. Every market-data result is **[REAL]**.

**Question.** The referee's second report (finding J1) notes that E12's test of up alarms after FOMC statements and CPI releases, the only pre-specified primary test of the real-data work (E20), used the plug-in baseline, which has no finite-sample guarantee, while the abstract says that the FOMC result shows what the guarantee buys. Does the result hold when the monitor is one that carries a proved per-day false alarm bound?

**Summary.**
* **The pre-registered primary test passes.** [REAL] With the confidence-sequence baseline restarted at every UTC day boundary (P1), an up alarm came within 6 hours of 8 of the 16 FOMC statements on BTC (50%, Wilson 95% interval 28% to 72%), against a matched control rate of 10.9%: a difference of 39.1 points, a ratio of 4.6, one-sided stratified permutation p = 0.00017, Holm p = 0.00033 in the primary family (`e22_tests.csv`, family F22a). E12's plug-in had 9 of 16 against 13.9%, Holm p = 0.00025.
* **CPI on BTC, the other member of the primary family, also passes under P1** [REAL]: 5 of 22 against 5.9%, p = 0.0097, Holm 0.0097. It is a secondary result, and a fragile one: the release count is the plug-in's (5 of 22); what changed is the matched control rate (11.7% under the plug-in). Without the daily restart (S1) the same cell gives 3 of 22, p = 0.12.
* **The confidence-sequence arms are not blind at most releases; they are watching at more releases than the plug-in.** [REAL] P1 was monitoring with an increase side able to alarm at 80 of the 114 coin-release pairs (70%), S1 at 77 (68%), the rank monitor S2 at all 114, the plug-in at 55 (48%). One BTC FOMC statement (29 January 2025) fell in a segment whose increase side could not alarm (τ² / m_up = 0.95), in both P1 and S1; the plug-in flagged it after 15 minutes.
* **The guarantee is a property of the monitor, not of these data.** [REAL] P1 raised an alarm in 48.1% to 53.5% of its monitored periods (a segment within one UTC day; bound 5% per period under the tolerance), 0.92 to 1.15 alarms per monitored day against a long-run bound of 0.0404. On real one-minute returns the ±25% tolerance of Theorem 6.4 does not hold on most days, so these alarms are not false alarms in the sense of the theorem, and E22 does not test the bound.
* **Reproduction.** [REAL] The plug-in arm rerun through the E22 script reproduces E12's published numbers exactly (60 test rows, 114 release windows and the monitor summaries; every compared value equal, `e22_reproduction.csv`), and S2 reproduces E14 Q14g's awake-B rows exactly.

### Design

Everything except the monitor is E12's, imported from `experiments/e12_crypto_events.py`: the 16 FOMC statements and 22 CPI releases of 2024 and 2025, Binance one-minute BTCUSDT, ETHUSDT and SOLUSDT returns over the predictable intraday profile (711 monitored days from 21 January 2024), the streaming design, the outcome (an up alarm within 6 hours of the release), the matched control windows (same weekday and US Eastern clock time, at least 2 days from any event day) and the exact one-sided stratified permutation test, with E12's stratified Fisher test as a cross-check.

| Arm | Monitor | Bound proved, and its hypothesis |
|---|---|---|
| P0 (reference) | E12's plug-in, `VolatilityMonitor(A = 28,800, c = 3, calibration 1440, band 0.25)` | none (nominal m / A = 5% for the first day of a segment if the baseline were the true one) |
| **P1 (primary)** | `PeriodicVolatilityMonitor(baseline="cs", delta=0.01, A = 36,000, period=1440)`, restart at 00:00 UTC (offset 0, checked), recalibration of 1440 minutes after each alarm | δ + m / A = **5% for every day of a segment**, marginally (not given the past), if the tolerance (H↑), (H↓) of `docs/math.md` Theorem 6.4 with b = 0.25 holds **to the end of that day** (Corollary 1 of `docs/theory_per_period.md`). Long run: (δ + M / A) / (1 - δ) alarms in M monitored minutes, 0.0404 per monitored day (Corollary 6.6; it applies to P1 because a restart only lowers the supermartingale of its proof) |
| S1 | the same without the daily restart, `VolatilityMonitor(baseline="cs", delta=0.01, A = 36,000)` | 5% for the **first** monitored day of each segment under the tolerance for that day (Theorem 6.4, part 1; part 4 adds P(tolerance fails) with no assumption); later days of a segment only δ + d m / A; long run as P1 |
| S2 | E14's awake rank monitor (awake-B: ranks of \|u\| among the segment's earlier values, A = 28,800, payoffs divided by 1.25, no blind period) | m / A = 5% for the first day after each restart if the segment's returns are exchangeable given the past (Theorem B.2, Remark B.3 of `docs/theory_running_tau.md`); long run 0.05 per day |

P1 runs E12's design as it stands; no substitute configuration was needed. Because recalibration takes 1440 minutes, the monitored minutes of each UTC day belong to one segment, so each UTC day is one period of Corollary 1 and P1 raises at most one alarm per day. P1 differs from P0 in three ways at once (baseline, A and the restart); S1 removes only the restart.

### The pre-registered tests [REAL]

Outcome: an up alarm within 6 hours, all releases (a release at which the monitor is calibrating or blind counts as one without an alarm). Holm within each family (`e22_tests.csv`, columns `family`, `p_holm_family`).

| Family | Arm | Coin | FOMC: releases with alarm | matched control rate | p | Holm p | CPI: releases with alarm | matched control rate | p | Holm p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| F22e (reference) | P0 plug-in | BTC | 9 / 16 | 13.9% | 0.00012 | 0.00025 | 5 / 22 | 11.7% | 0.11 | 0.11 |
| **F22a (primary)** | **P1** | **BTC** | **8 / 16** | **10.9%** | **0.00017** | **0.00033** | 5 / 22 | 5.9% | 0.0097 | 0.0097 |
| F22b | P1 | ETH | 9 / 16 | 9.5% | 0.0000067 | 0.000020 | 6 / 22 | 11.6% | 0.038 | 0.075 |
| | P1 | SOL | 10 / 16 | 12.0% | 0.0000042 | 0.000017 | 4 / 22 | 6.1% | 0.046 | 0.075 |
| F22c | S1 | BTC | 8 / 16 | 12.4% | 0.00040 | 0.0020 | 3 / 22 | 5.5% | 0.12 | 0.12 |
| | S1 | ETH | 7 / 16 | 9.5% | 0.00050 | 0.0020 | 8 / 22 | 11.3% | 0.0023 | 0.0069 |
| | S1 | SOL | 11 / 16 | 12.1% | 0.00000038 | 0.0000023 | 4 / 22 | 6.1% | 0.045 | 0.090 |
| F22d | S2 | BTC | 13 / 16 | 18.8% | 0.00000020 | 0.0000012 | 10 / 22 | 13.0% | 0.00027 | 0.00080 |
| | S2 | ETH | 10 / 16 | 18.8% | 0.00020 | 0.00079 | 11 / 22 | 16.8% | 0.00039 | 0.00080 |
| | S2 | SOL | 12 / 16 | 18.5% | 0.0000023 | 0.000011 | 10 / 22 | 13.8% | 0.00042 | 0.00080 |

The exact stratified Fisher test agrees with the permutation test (P1, BTC: FOMC 0.0014, CPI 0.020). Every FOMC cell of families F22a to F22d holds after Holm. CPI holds after Holm on BTC under P1 and in every S2 cell; it does not hold on ETH and SOL under P1 (Holm 0.075) or on BTC and SOL under S1. S2's rows are E14 Q14g's published result, reproduced to the last digit; they add no confirmatory evidence.

### Alarm rate per day against the bound [REAL]

`e22_monitor_summary.csv`. "Per-day share" is, for P1, the share of monitored periods (a segment within one UTC day) with an alarm, whose long-run expectation is at most (m + κ)/(A (1 - δ)) = 4.04% under the tolerance in every segment (each period has probability at most δ + m/A = 5% by Corollary 1; the share pools periods selected by earlier alarms, so its bound comes from counting, round 10 review m5; `docs/theory_blind_guard.md`, Corollary 2); for the other arms it is the share of segments with an alarm within their first 1440 monitored minutes, the quantity Theorem 6.4 part 1, Theorem B.2 and (nominally) Theorem B bound. Wilson intervals treat periods and segments as independent and are descriptive only.

| Arm | Alarms per UTC day (BTC, ETH, SOL) | Alarms per monitored day | Long-run bound per monitored day | Per-day share (BTC, ETH, SOL) | Bound on the per-day share |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P0 plug-in | 0.70, 0.69, 0.67 | 2.35, 2.26, 1.99 | 0.05 (nominal) | 91.6%, 88.8%, 89.0% (first day) | 5% (nominal) |
| **P1** | 0.52, 0.53, 0.48 | 1.10, 1.15, 0.92 | 0.0404 | **52.5%, 53.5%, 48.1%** (per period; lower Wilson limits 48.9%, 49.8%, 44.4%) | **5%** |
| S1 | 0.54, 0.55, 0.50 | 1.17, 1.21, 0.99 | 0.0404 | 71.0%, 68.6%, 62.7% (first day) | 5% |
| S2 | 0.93, 0.80, 0.65 | 0.93, 0.80, 0.65 | 0.05 | 58.7%, 52.4%, 42.2% (first day) | 5% |

Every arm alarms about 10 to 47 times more often than its bound allows under its null. The monitors are not at fault: the nulls exclude volatility that moves by more than 25% (or is not exchangeable) within a day, which is the normal state of one-minute crypto returns (TH6, E19). The numbers say how far real days are from the null, not how often the monitors raise false alarms.

### Share of releases watched [REAL]

A release is *watched* if the monitor is monitoring at its minute and, for the X-based arms, the segment's increase side can alarm (E19's blind-segment criterion: off when τ² ≤ m_up = U (1 + b)); for S2 watched means monitoring. `e22_watched.csv`, `e22_windows.csv`.

| Arm | FOMC watched (BTC, ETH, SOL; of 16) | CPI watched (of 22) | All 114 | Monitoring but blind | Matched control windows watched at the anchor |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P0 plug-in | 9, 8, 9 | 9, 8, 12 | 55 (48%) | 0 | 32.9% to 42.6% |
| **P1** | 10, 12, 13 | 16, 13, 16 | **80 (70%)** | 1 | 59.5% to 70.1% |
| S1 | 10, 10, 14 | 14, 15, 14 | 77 (68%) | 1 | 58.5% to 65.7% |
| S2 | 16, 16, 16 | 22, 22, 22 | 114 (100%) | 0 | 100% |

E19's blind-segment diagnostic over the whole runs: P1 had one BTC segment of 373 with the increase side off (3.25 days, 0.96% of its monitored time) and none on ETH or SOL; S1 two BTC segments of 383 (5.19 and 3.25 days, 2.6%) and none on ETH or SOL; the plug-in none. The decrease side was never off. Median τ² / m_up over segments: 5.09 to 5.63 for P1 (10% quantile 2.67 to 3.40), 5.30 to 5.80 for the plug-in. The confidence-sequence arms are not blind at most releases: they monitor more of the time than the plug-in (45% to 52% of minutes against 30% to 33%) because they alarm less often and so recalibrate less often. On BTC every release with a P1 up alarm within 6 hours was watched at its minute (8 of the 10 watched FOMC statements, 5 of the 16 watched CPI releases; `up_within_6h_when_watched`). The mean share of the 6-hour window watched is low after FOMC statements (P1: 28% to 31%) because the alarm itself starts a 1440-minute recalibration.

### Exploratory, reported raw [REAL]

Not part of any family; no decision attached (`status` column of `e22_tests.csv`).
* Up alarm within 1 hour, all releases, P1: BTC FOMC 7 of 16 against 0.09% of matched control windows (p = 1.4 × 10⁻¹²); BTC CPI 3 of 22 against 1.2% (p = 0.0032).
* Releases watched at their minute, with controls also watched, P1: BTC FOMC 8 of 10 against 13.4% (p = 8.0 × 10⁻⁶); BTC CPI 5 of 16 against 9.4% (p = 0.016). E12's restriction to releases at which the monitor was calibrated ("monitoring at start") is also in the file, computed by E12's function.
* *Not pre-registered, descriptive:* median minutes from a BTC FOMC statement to the first up alarm, among statements with one: P0 15, P1 40.5, S1 40.5, S2 20. The confidence-sequence arms bet against the upper confidence bound times 1.25, a higher baseline than the plug-in's, and alarm later.
* *Post hoc, descriptive:* at the 16 BTC FOMC statements P1 and the plug-in agree on 9 (both flag 5, neither flags 4). P1 flagged three statements at which the plug-in was recalibrating (31 January, 12 June and 31 July 2024); it missed one in its blind segment (29 January 2025) and three at which it was itself recalibrating (18 December 2024, 30 July and 29 October 2025), all of which the plug-in flagged.

### Reading

* **E12's FOMC result does not depend on the plug-in baseline.** With a monitor whose false alarm probability is proved to be at most 5% in each day of a segment (under a ±25% tolerance on the conditional truncated variance up to the end of that day), the pre-registered test gives the same answer as E12: 8 of 16 FOMC statements on BTC were followed by an up alarm within six hours, against 10.9% of matched control times (Holm p = 0.00033). The FOMC contrast also holds on ETH and SOL, without the daily restart, and with the rank monitor, in every cell after Holm.
* **What it does not show.** It does not show that the bound holds on these data: the same monitor alarmed in about half of its monitored days, ten times its budget, so the tolerance fails on most real days and the bound is not in force there. It does not show that the alarms after FOMC statements mark lasting changes. And the abstract's phrase "what the guarantee buys" should be read as "the result holds for a monitor that carries the guarantee", not as evidence that the guarantee was exercised.
* **CPI.** On BTC the CPI cell passes under P1 (Holm 0.0097) where it failed under the plug-in (0.11), but the release count is unchanged at 5 of 22; the matched control rate halved. Without the daily restart it fails again (3 of 22, p = 0.12), and on ETH and SOL under P1 it does not survive Holm. CPI evidence therefore depends on the configuration; only the FOMC evidence is robust to it.
* **Blindness.** The concern that the confidence-sequence baseline is blind at most releases (E19's blind segments) does not materialise here: one release in 114 fell in a blind segment, and the confidence-sequence arms watched 68% to 70% of releases against 48% for the plug-in.

### Caveats

* The data and E12's results were known when E22 was designed; S2's result was published in E14 Q14g; S1's alarm list over 21 January 2024 to 30 June 2025 is identical to E19's committed confidence-sequence list at band 0.25 for the three coins (285, 290 and 260 alarms; checked post hoc, `results/e19_cs_events.csv`). The pre-registration fixes the configuration and the test, not the novelty of the data.
* Sixteen FOMC statements: the Wilson interval of P1's BTC rate runs from 28% to 72%. The three coins move together and are not independent replications.
* P1 changes the baseline, A and the restart together; S1 isolates the restart. The restart at 00:00 UTC falls 5 hours into the 6-hour window of FOMC statements made in US Eastern standard time (19:00 UTC); matched controls in daylight saving months start at 18:00 UTC and do not cross it. The restart only lowers the statistic.
* The bound of Corollary 1 is marginal and per segment: given the observed past (for example, no alarm yet) it is P(Gᶜ | past) + m / A, which can exceed 5%. Its hypothesis is a tolerance that real days violate; part 4 of Theorem 6.4, which charges the probability of violation, is proved for the first m steps of a segment (S1), not stated for the restarted monitor.
* The deseasonalising profile uses past days only, so it is known before each minute and the hypotheses are statements about the deseasonalised return; its accuracy affects whether the tolerance holds, not the validity of the theorem.

## E23. E22's release test on fresh releases: the FOMC statements and CPI releases of 2026

Script `experiments/e23_fresh_releases.py`; pre-registration `docs/preregistration_e23.md` (commit `b5c1573`, 06:35:40 UTC on 3 November 2026, committed alone with the event file `data/events/us_macro_events_2026.csv` before any Binance return of 2026 was downloaded or loaded); outputs `results/e23_*.csv` and `results/figures/e23_release_rates.png`; tests `tests/test_e23.py` [SYNTHETIC]; iteration notes `docs/iterations/E23.md`. Every market-data result is **[REAL]**; the power calculation is **[SYNTHETIC]** (a simulation whose inputs are E22's real rates).

**Question.** Every real-data result on FOMC statements and CPI releases so far (E12, E14 Q14g, E22) used the releases of 2024 and 2025, and E22 was designed after E12's answer was known. Does E22's pre-registered result hold on releases nobody in the project had looked at: the FOMC statements and CPI releases of January to October 2026?

**Summary.**
* **The pre-registered primary test fails.** [REAL] With P1 (the confidence-sequence baseline restarted at every UTC day boundary, E22's primary monitor), an up alarm came within 6 hours of 2 of the 16 FOMC statements and CPI releases of 2026 on BTC (12.5%, Wilson 95% interval 3.5% to 36.0%), against a mean matched control rate of 5.9%: a ratio of 2.1, one-sided stratified permutation p = 0.25 (Fisher cross-check 0.29; `e23_tests.csv`, family F23a). The planned power was 0.82 at E22's rates for the 17 releases expected, and 0.78 for the 16 that the data cover (`e23_power.csv`, `e23_power_actual.csv`). E12's and E22's release contrast is **not confirmed** on fresh releases.
* **No P1 secondary family passes.** [REAL] The pooled test on ETH (4 of 16, p = 0.067) and SOL (5 of 16, p = 0.039) gives Holm 0.079 for both (F23b); none of the six FOMC and CPI cells passes Holm (F23c; best SOL FOMC, 3 of 6, p = 0.079, Holm 0.48). The FOMC part on BTC was 1 of 6 statements (16.7%) against 10.3%; in 2024 and 2025 it was 8 of 16 against 10.9%.
* **The rank monitor, which is never blind, still sees the FOMC statements.** [REAL] S2 (E14's awake rank monitor) flagged 4 of the 6 FOMC statements within 6 hours on each coin, Holm p = 0.016 (BTC), 0.033 (ETH), 0.055 (SOL) in its pre-registered secondary family (F23e); its CPI cells fail on every coin. The plug-in passes one cell (ETH FOMC, 4 of 6, Holm 0.040). These are secondary results and cannot rescue the primary test.
* **On BTC, P1 was blind or recalibrating at 5 of the 16 releases, and alarmed after only 2 of the 11 it watched.** [REAL] Two BTC segments could not raise an increase alarm (τ² ≤ m_up): 10 to 15 August and 17 August to 3 October 2026 (47 days), 28% of P1's monitored time on BTC; they held the CPI releases of 12 August and 11 September and the FOMC statement of 16 September. In 2024 and 2025 one BTC release in 38 fell in a blind segment and 13 of the 26 watched BTC releases were followed by an up alarm.
* **The per-day bound is far from the observed alarm rates, as in E22.** [REAL] P1 alarmed in 37.8%, 48.0% and 46.0% of its monitored periods (a segment within one UTC day; BTC, ETH, SOL) against the 5% bound that holds under the ±25% tolerance; the tolerance fails on most real days, so these are alarm rates, not false alarm rates.

### Design

Everything is E22's and E12's code: each (coin, arm) run is `E22.job` itself, after E23 sets E12's period and event file and adds the inclusion rule. A gate run first (`e23_gate.csv`): with E12's own period and events, the switch reproduced E22's committed P1 BTC rows exactly (30 test rows of 14 columns, 38 window rows of 27 columns, the alarm and period counts; 0 mismatches), and the pooled function, restricted to one release type, reproduced E12's per-type test to the last digit for every arm, coin, type and both outcomes (`e23_pooled_check.csv`, 48 rows, 0 mismatches).

| Item | E23 |
|---|---|
| Releases | `data/events/us_macro_events_2026.csv`, each date checked by web search on 3 November 2026 against the Federal Reserve press release and the BLS release (archive page, or BLS regional releases of the same date for 11 September; the official hosts do not resolve from this machine, so search results that index them were used). 7 FOMC statements (14:00 ET: 28 January, 18 March, 29 April, 17 June, 29 July, 16 September, 28 October) and 10 CPI releases (08:30 ET: 13 January, 13 February (moved from 11 February by the lapse in appropriations that began on 31 January 2026), 11 March, 10 April, 12 May, 10 June, 14 July, 12 August, 11 September, 14 October). No unscheduled FOMC statement was found; E12's rule (second day of each scheduled meeting) would exclude one. |
| Inclusion | A release counts if its 6-hour window ends at or before the data end. The data end at 24 October 2026 23:59 UTC (the mirror's October file stops there; no November file), so the FOMC statement of 28 October is excluded (`e23_events_excluded.csv`): **16 releases, 6 FOMC and 10 CPI**. |
| Data | Binance spot one-minute bars, BTCUSDT, ETHUSDT, SOLUSDT; loaded from 12 December 2025 (20 days of intraday-profile warm-up, as E12), monitored from 1 January 2026 00:00 UTC, 297 days, 427,680 minutes per coin. No duplicate timestamps, no missing minute, no non-positive price, no NaN return in the monitored period (`e23_data_checks.csv`, `e23_data_gaps.csv` empty). |
| Controls | E12's `control_anchors`: same weekday and US Eastern clock time, at least 2 days from every event day, 48-hour follow-up inside the data. 29 per release (Wednesday 14:00, Tuesday and Wednesday 08:30) and 39 (Friday 08:30). |
| Arms | P1 (primary) `PeriodicVolatilityMonitor(baseline="cs", delta=0.01, A = 36,000, period=1440)`, restart at 00:00 UTC (offset 0, checked); P0 E12's plug-in (A = 28,800); S2 E14's awake rank monitor (A = 28,800, seed 14,000); S1 P1 without the restart. Bounds as in E22. |
| Primary test | Chosen before any 2026 return was loaded, by the power calculation below: one stratified permutation test over BTC's FOMC and CPI releases together (each release its own stratum with its own matched controls), one-sided, pass if p ≤ 0.05. |

**Power, planned before the data** [SYNTHETIC] (`e23_power.csv`; 20,000 replications, seed 23,000; releases and control windows Bernoulli with E22's P1 BTC rates, controls shared within each weekday-and-time group as in the data):

| Scenario | BTC FOMC alone | BTC FOMC and CPI together |
|---|---|---|
| E22's rates (FOMC 50% vs 10.9%, CPI 22.7% vs 5.9%), 17 releases planned | 0.690 | **0.818** |
| the same, 16 releases in the data (`e23_power_actual.csv`) | 0.625 | **0.779** |
| half of E22's excess, 17 releases (16) | 0.330 (0.284) | 0.405 (0.374) |
| E22's FOMC rates, no CPI effect, 17 releases (16) | 0.690 (0.625) | 0.534 (0.451) |
| null, 17 releases (16) | 0.058 (0.047) | 0.039 (0.036) |

The null line shows a property of E12's test found while planning: when the releases of one group share their control windows, treating their strata as independent can exceed the nominal level slightly (5.8% for seven FOMC statements sharing 29 controls, Monte Carlo s.e. 0.17 points; 4.7% for six); the pooled test stays below 5%.

### The pre-registered tests [REAL]

Outcome: an up alarm within 6 hours, all releases (calibrating or blind counts as no alarm). Holm within each family (`e23_tests.csv`, columns `family`, `p_holm_family`).

### Exploratory, reported raw [REAL]

Not part of any family; no decision attached (`status` column of `e23_tests.csv`).
* The pooled test for the other arms: S2 6 of 16 (BTC, p = 0.0070), 7 of 16 (ETH, 0.0025), 7 of 16 (SOL, 0.0083); P0 2, 7 and 2 of 16 (p = 0.55, 0.0018, 0.59); S1 2, 4 and 5 of 16 (p = 0.18, 0.051, 0.032).
* Up alarm within 1 hour, pooled, P1: BTC 2 of 16 against 0.86% of matched control windows (p = 0.015), ETH 2 of 16 (p = 0.045), SOL 3 of 16 (p = 0.0078). S2: 6, 7 and 7 of 16 against 2.2% to 3.2% (p at most 1.3 × 10⁻⁵). The few alarms that do come after a release come quickly.
* No P1 up alarm in the 6 hours before any BTC release (`up_pre`: 0 of 16; controls 3.5% to 6.4%).
* *Descriptive:* median minutes from release to the first up alarm, among releases with one: P1 BTC 26 (both alarms, 14 July CPI and 29 July FOMC); S2 FOMC 9 (BTC), 7 (ETH), 8 (SOL); S2 CPI 10, 11, 7 (`e23_delay.csv`).
* *Post hoc, descriptive:* the releases moved the market less than in 2024 and 2025: the median ratio of the mean absolute deseasonalised return in the first hour after a BTC release to that of the 6 hours before was 2.11 for FOMC and 1.73 for CPI in 2026, against 2.51 and 2.00 in 2024 and 2025 (`abs_ret_first_hour_over_pre` in `e23_windows.csv` and `e22_windows.csv`).

### Reading

* **The confirmatory test did not confirm.** The reading fixed in advance applies: the release contrast is not confirmed on fresh releases. With power 0.78 at E22's rates for the 16 releases available, a failure would happen with probability about 0.22 if those rates were true and about 0.63 if the true excess were half of E22's; the result says that in 2026 the contrast under P1 on BTC was smaller than in 2024 and 2025 or absent, not that it is absent. E12's and E22's FOMC result for the monitor with a per-day guarantee rests on data that were known when E22 was designed, and the README and the paper must say that the one confirmatory test did not confirm it.
* **Why, descriptively (no test attached).** Both of the mechanisms named in the pre-registration contributed on BTC: P1 was blind or recalibrating at 5 of 16 releases (in 2024 and 2025: 6 of 22 CPI and 6 of 16 FOMC releases were not watched, but only one was blind), and it alarmed after 2 of the 11 releases it watched (13 of 26 in 2024 and 2025). The blind segment of 17 August to 3 October is the failure mode of E19 on a fresh stream: a segment whose truncation level τ² falls below the increase side's threshold m_up cannot alarm upward until a down alarm ends it, and on BTC that took 47 days.
* **What still holds.** The awake rank monitor, which carries a 5% bound on the first day after each restart under exchangeability and is never blind, flagged 4 of 6 FOMC statements on every coin, with Holm p at most 0.055 in its pre-registered secondary family. This agrees with the FOMC contrast of 2024 and 2025 (E14 Q14g: 13 of 16 on BTC) but is secondary: it cannot replace the primary test, and its alarms are no more than an alarm rate of 0.70 to 0.82 per day allows. No arm shows a CPI contrast on any coin in 2026.

### Caveats

* Sixteen releases on one coin: the Wilson interval of the primary rate runs from 3.5% to 36.0%. ETH and SOL move with BTC and are not independent replications.
* The data stop on 24 October 2026, a week short of the planned end, so the FOMC statement of 28 October is out by the pre-registered inclusion rule; the power at the actual count is reported above.
* The bound of Corollary 1 is not tested by E23: on these days its hypothesis (the ±25% tolerance) fails most of the time.
* The power calculation assumes independent release and control outcomes; real alarms cluster in time, so the true power may differ.

## E24. A proved guard against blind segments of the confidence-sequence baseline, and a forward pre-registration

Theory `docs/theory_blind_guard.md`; code `src/avmonitor/guard.py`; script `experiments/e24_blind_guard.py` (parts `theory`, `selection`, `synthetic`, `real`, `e19blind`, `power`, `future`, `figs`); outputs `results/e24_*.csv` and `results/figures/e24_*.png`; tests `tests/test_guard.py` [SYNTHETIC]; forward pre-registration `docs/preregistration_e24_future.md` with `data/events/us_macro_events_e24_future.csv`; iteration notes `docs/iterations/E24.md`. Labels: [PROVED], [NUMERICAL], [SYNTHETIC], [REAL]; every real-data result here is **post hoc and exploratory**, because the data were seen by E19, E22 and E23 before the guard was designed.

**Question.** In E23 the primary monitor P1 could not raise an increase alarm for 28% of its monitored time on BTC, and 3 of the 16 releases of 2026 fell in such blind segments. E19 had proposed a guard (discard a blind calibration window and calibrate again) and left it unproved, because the kept windows are selected by their bounds. Can the guard be proved, what does it cost, does it help, and what test on releases nobody has seen would settle the release question?

**Summary.**
* **The guard is proved, and the naive version is not.** [PROVED] A blind segment (τ² ≤ m↑) is decided when calibration ends, so a guard can act on it. Discarding blind windows and calibrating again breaks the per-window coverage of the kept window's bounds (Proposition 3: under a law inside the tolerance relative to the kept window, a window before the K-th is kept exactly when its upper bound fails), but spending the error budget over the windows tried, δ_1 + ... + δ_K ≤ δ, gives P(the kept window's bounds fail) ≤ δ (Theorem 1), and with it Theorem 6.4, Corollary 6.6 and the per-day Corollary 1 unchanged, with the tolerance taken relative to the kept window (Theorem 2). That null depends on the guard's tuning through the selection; the tolerance relative to each of the K windows, (H*), is a selection-free sufficient condition that implies both the guarded and the unguarded hypotheses. A fallback to the rank monitor after K blind windows keeps δ + m/A under a mixed hypothesis (Theorem 3). [NUMERICAL] For P1's window the construction triples the failure probability with three windows and no spending (7.6 × 10⁻⁴ against 2.5 × 10⁻⁴; `e24_selection.csv`), which is still below δ = 0.01; the naive guard exceeds δ on this law only from about 40 windows, and with no cap on the number of windows the kept window's bound fails with probability 1.
* **Blind is not the only failure: near-blind windows are just as deaf.** [PROVED, SYNTHETIC] With ρ = τ²/m↑ ≤ 1.0105 P1's increase side cannot alarm within a day whatever the data; with a step in volatility of 4 or 6 after the τ part (ρ ≈ 1.2 and 1.03) the unguarded P1 and the guard with E19's criterion (η = 0) detected a later doubling within a day in at most 16% of paths, the guard with η = 0.25 in 86.5% and 100% (`e24_synthetic.csv`).
* **Recommended guard: K = 3, budgets δ/2, δ/4, δ/4, η = 0.25, rank fallback** (chosen among the guarded monitors from the synthetic results, before any real-data rerun; η = 0.25 and K = 3 were set before the synthetic run, after a scratch look at P1's real BTC windows; `docs/theory_blind_guard.md` 6.1). [SYNTHETIC] No alarm in the first day or any of the first four days of a null segment in 800 paths of any constant-law design, for any monitor (upper limit 0.0037; bound 0.05); detection within a day 86.5% to 100% where the unguarded P1 had 0% to 0.25%; cost: one extra calibration day only where the first window is near-blind.
* **On real data the guard removes every blind segment at a small cost.** [REAL, post hoc] It acted only on BTC (3 windows in 711 days of 2024 to 2025, 5 in 297 days of 2026; no fallback needed); no monitored minute of the guarded P1 was blind, against 28% for P1 on BTC in 2026. All 8 discarded windows began on a weekend: the τ part was a quiet weekend stretch, in three 2026 windows with a median absolute return of exactly one price tick, and the sequence part was 5 to 1010 times more volatile. In E19's diagnostic (no daily restart) the guard turned BTC's 83% blind time (band 0.5, one segment of 136 days) into 0%, with one discarded window; the unguarded rows reproduce E19's exactly (`e24_e19_blind.csv`).
* **The guard does not rescue E23's primary test, and nothing here is confirmatory.** [REAL, post hoc, exploratory] On BTC in 2026 the guarded P1 had 4 of 16 releases with an up alarm within 6 hours against a matched control rate of 8.9% (raw p = 0.056; FOMC 3 of 6), P1 2 of 16 (p = 0.25), the rank monitor S2 6 of 16 (p = 0.007). These data were seen and the guard was designed after E23 failed.
* **A forward test is pre-registered** (`docs/preregistration_e24_future.md`, commit `22f1988`, 08:46 UTC, 3 November 2026, before any return after 24 October 2026 was loaded). By a rule committed before the power part ran (a scratch power check of S2 alone, 2,000 replications, preceded it; `docs/iterations/E24.md`, iteration 4), the primary test is **S2, BTC FOMC statements and CPI releases pooled, 25 October 2026 to 1 June 2027 (11 planned releases), power 0.82 at the pooled 2024 to 2026 rates** [SYNTHETIC; planning inputs REAL]; 0.60 at the 2026 rates, 0.37 at half the pooled excess. The script refuses to run before 1 June 2027, on data that end earlier, or while any release is unverified; after the round 10 review it also refuses when a scheduled FOMC row has been deleted, when a release is marked verified before it happened, or when the pipeline no longer reproduces E23's committed rows (a disclosed amendment that only adds refusals).


### Theory [PROVED] (`docs/theory_blind_guard.md`)

| Statement | Content |
|---|---|
| Lemma 1, Proposition 1 | A segment is blind when τ² ≤ m↑ = (1 + b) Ū_T: every increase factor is at most 1, so the increase side cannot alarm within 2A - 1 monitored steps of a (re)start, and with P1's daily restart (carry 0) never. The event is in F_T (T, the end of calibration, is a stopping time), so the guard can act on it. |
| Proposition 2 | Near-blind, ρ = τ²/m↑ ≤ 1 + η: the exact floor d_min(ρ) on the steps to an increase alarm after a (re)start, over all data, attained by X ≡ τ², and a bound log(1 + λ_max η) on the expected log growth per step under any law. For P1 no increase alarm is possible within a day when ρ ≤ 1.0105; d_min = 1503 steps at ρ = 1.01, 371 at 1.05, 91 at 1.25 [NUMERICAL, `e24_near_blind.csv`, figure `e24_near_blind.png`]. |
| Theorem 1 | Retry guard with error spending: windows k = 1, ..., K with budgets δ_k, Σδ_k ≤ δ; discard a near-blind window and calibrate again; then P(the kept window's bounds fail given the past) ≤ Σ_k δ_k P(window k is tried) ≤ δ, for any discard rule decided at the end of each window. |
| Proposition 3 | The selection is real: under a law inside the tolerance relative to the kept window (not relative to the discarded ones), a window before the K-th is kept exactly when its upper bound fails. With no cap on the number of windows (E19's proposal) the kept window's bound fails with probability 1; with a cap K and the same δ for every window it fails with probability 1 - Π_k(1 - p(δ)), about K times one window's, which for P1's window exceeds δ only from about 40 windows (p(δ) is about 1/20 of δ/2). Spending makes the bound hold for every law and every K. |
| Theorem 2 | Theorem 6.4 and Corollary 6.6 of `docs/math.md` and Corollary 1 of `docs/theory_per_period.md` hold unchanged with δ the total budget, T the end of the kept window and the tolerance relative to the kept window's sequence part. The kept window depends on δ_k, the bets and η, so this null depends on the guard's tuning, and the guarded and unguarded monitors test different nulls; the tolerance relative to each of the K windows, (H*), is a selection-free sufficient condition that implies both (part 4), and it holds under a constant conditional law from the end of the first τ part (covers a step in volatility inside it). |
| Proposition 4 | Time-out after D periods: per-segment bounds unchanged; long-run bound grows by δ/D alarms per period. |
| Theorem 3 | Fallback to E14's awake rank monitor after K near-blind windows: P(alarm within m monitored steps of a segment) ≤ Σδ_k + m/A, where the cs branch needs the tolerance relative to the kept window and the rank branch needs exchangeability of the returns after the fallback given the past; the per-period and long-run bounds carry over (the latter by a per-segment optional-stopping argument). |
| Remark 6 | Not specific to the guard: Corollary 1 bounds a period of a segment; for a fixed calendar day the bound is δ E[segments started by then] + (m + κ)/A, which under the tolerance in every segment is at most δ(1 + (δ + d m/A)/(1 - δ)) + (m + κ)/A on the d-th day (P1: 5.05% on day 1, 6.02% on day 25, 9.05% on day 100) [PROVED]; whether a null attains more than δ + (m + κ)/A on some day is open. |
| Corollary 2 | Not specific to the guard: under the tolerance in every segment, E[N_M] ≤ (δ + ((m + κ)/A) E\|𝒫_M\|)/(1 - δ), with 𝒫_M the periods holding one of the first M monitored steps; so the long-run share of alarmed periods (a ratio of expectations) is at most (m + κ)/(A(1 - δ)) = 4.04% for P1. This, not the 5% of Corollary 1, is the bound for the per-day shares of E22, E23 and this experiment. |

### Synthetic experiments [SYNTHETIC] (`e24_synthetic.csv`, `e24_synthetic_paths.csv.gz`, figure `e24_synthetic.png`)

Eleven-day streams of one-minute returns; the standard deviation doubles at a uniform minute of day 9; 800 paths per design; five monitors on the same paths: U, P1 unguarded (`PeriodicVolatilityMonitor(baseline="cs", delta=0.01, A = 36,000, period=1440)`, band 0.25); G, guarded, K = 3, η = 0, keep; GR, as G with the rank fallback; GE, K = 3, η = 0.25, rank fallback (the recommendation); R, E22's rank monitor S2 (A = 28,800). Null endpoints use each monitor's first segment that starts after the pre-change law has settled (after the first 360 minutes for the steps and `frozen`, after the first day for `drift8_gauss`). GR gave the same numbers as G everywhere (no fallback was needed).

| Design | Median ρ of the first window (U) | U's blind share | Detected within a day: U / G / GE / R | Median delay (min): G / GE / R | Extra calibration, GE (min per path) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| step2_gauss: sd 1 for 360 min, then 2 | 2.09 | 0 | 100 / 100 / 100 / 100% | 144 / 144 / 25 | 0 |
| step4_gauss | 1.20 | 0 | 0.25 / 0.1 / 86.5 / 100% | 1048 / 49 / 27 | 1244 |
| step6_gauss | 1.03 | 13% | 0 / 16.2 / 100 / 100% | 48 / 50 / 26 | 1440 |
| step8_gauss | 0.96 | 99% | 0 / 99.2 / 100 / 100% | 50 / 50 / 27 | 1440 |
| step8_t3 (Student t3) | 0.96 | 97.5% | 0 / 97.9 / 100 / 99.8% | 115 / 115 / 127 | 1440 |
| frozen: ticks, 60% frozen minutes in the first 360, then 10% | 0.88 | 100% | 0 / 100 / 100 / 100% | 64 / 64 / 30 | 1440 |
| drift8_gauss: sd rises 1 to 8 over the first day | 1.61 | 0 | 100 / 100 / 100 / 100% | 48 / 48 / 25 | 0 |
| calm_btc_days: E19's calm BTC days, shuffled whole | 4.72 | 0 | 67 / 66 / 66 / 88% | 220 / 221 / 90 | 0 |
| calm_btc_perm: the same returns, permuted | 4.17 | 0 | 100 / 100 / 100 / 100% | 111 / 111 / 93 | 0 |

* **Null rates.** In the seven designs whose law is constant after the first τ part (the five steps, `frozen`, `calm_btc_perm`) no monitor raised an alarm in the first day, or in any of the first four days, of its first null segment: 0 of 800 paths (one-sided 95% upper limit 0.0037) against the bound δ + m/A = 0.05 (R: 0 of 710 to 800 paths with a null segment; in `frozen` only 4, because its first segment starts before the frozen share falls). Expected alarms per path before the change are bounded by 0.27 to 0.31 (cs) and 0.37 to 0.42 (R); observed 0. The bounds hold with a wide margin, as in E19 and E22; the designs cannot rank the monitors by false alarms.
* **Where the hypotheses fail.** In `drift8_gauss` the first window is not near-blind (ρ ≈ 1.6) and is kept; every cs monitor alarms on the first monitored day of every path, which the theorem allows because its tolerance fails relative to that window. In `calm_btc_days` the level changes at day boundaries and every monitor alarms early (first-day share 0.78 U, 0.76 guarded, 0.62 R; 4.4 to 8.1 alarms per path): alarm rates, not false alarm rates.
* **What the guard buys.** Blindness disappears (blind share 0 for every guarded monitor in every design), and with η = 0.25 so does near-blindness. The rank monitor detects faster in eight of the nine designs (median 25 to 30 minutes against 48 to 64 for GE in step6, step8, frozen and drift8; 25 against 144 in step2), and slower under Student t3 returns (127 against 115); it is never blind. The guarded P1 keeps the tolerance-based per-day bound.

### Proposition 3 in numbers [NUMERICAL] (`e24_selection.csv`)

Under the construction of Proposition 3 (b = 0.25, η = 0, so a window is kept exactly when U_T < 0.8):

| Configuration | One window | 3 windows, δ each | 3 windows, halving (Theorem 1) |
|---|---|---|---|
| P1's window (n_cs = 1080, δ = 0.01; 400,000 replications per level) | 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ | 7.6 × 10⁻⁴ | 1.9 × 10⁻⁴ |
| illustration (n_cs = 150, δ = 0.3 per window; 200,000) | 0.0139 | 0.041 | 0.0063 |
| the same through `GuardedVolatilityMonitor` (4000 paths) | | 0.043 (s.e. 0.0032; formula 0.041; 0.0426 with that run's own p = 0.0144) | |

The selection multiplies the failure probability by the number of windows tried. On this law the naive guard with three windows still stays below δ (7.6 × 10⁻⁴ against 0.01; 0.041 against 0.3), because one window's sequence fails far less often than its budget δ/2; it exceeds δ from about 40 windows (26 in the illustration), and with no cap the kept window's bound fails with probability 1. Spending keeps the failure probability below δ for every law and every K. The round 10 review recomputed p(δ) with 1,000,000 replications per level (2.59 × 10⁻⁴ for P1's window, so K = 39; δ/2 is 19, 23 and 32 times p(δ) at δ = 0.01, 0.005 and 0.0025; `docs/review/round10_scripts/outputs/r10_selection.txt`).

The unguarded rows reproduce `e19_blind.csv` exactly (33 rows, 8 columns, 0 mismatches). ### Reading

The retry guard with error spending is a proved fix for blind segments of the confidence-sequence baseline: it keeps every bound of the unguarded monitor, under a hypothesis stated relative to the window it keeps, and on real BTC data it removes all blind time at the cost of about one calibration day per four months. The selection that E19 worried about is real (Proposition 3: with no cap it makes the kept window's bound fail with probability 1, and with a cap it multiplies the failure probability by up to the number of windows) and is paid for by splitting δ, not argued away. The hypothesis is relative to the window kept, which depends on the guard's tuning; the tolerance relative to every window tried is a selection-free condition under which both the guarded and the unguarded bounds hold. The guard does not, on the data already seen, restore the 2024 to 2025 release rates in 2026, and the rank monitor remains the stronger release detector; whether either result holds on new releases is now a pre-registered question with a fixed date.

### Caveats and what failed

* All real-data comparisons here are post hoc on seen data; the guard was designed after E23's failure, partly from E23's BTC windows.
* The synthetic null checks cannot separate the monitors (no alarm at all); the bounds are far from tight in these designs.
* The near-blind margin η = 0.25 and K = 3 were fixed before the synthetic run (commit `4c294e4`), after a 3-path smoke run and after iteration 1's scratch look at P1's 2026 BTC windows with ρ ≤ 1.2; other values were not explored. The design `frozen` and the null-segment filter were committed with the results.
* The first version of the per-period summary counted an empty first period (segments starting on a day boundary); fixed in the summary before any number was reported (iteration 2).
* Iteration 1's scratch look at P1's blind BTC windows attributed them all to tick-level τ parts; the committed account on the guarded monitor's windows (8 windows, two mechanisms) is in `e24_real_guard_windows.csv`, and the synthetic design `frozen` was chosen after that first look.
* The forward test's power rests on planning rates that include 2024 and 2025, when release rates were higher than in 2026; its power at the 2026 rates is 0.60. The official schedule pages could not be fetched; the 2027 dates rest on search results that index them.
* Whether an adaptive null exceeds δ + (m + κ)/A on a fixed calendar day (Remark 6) is open; the earlier sketch of such a null was withdrawn after the round 10 review, because a null cannot end good segments quickly.
* The round 10 review (`docs/review/independent_review_round10_e24.md`) found Proposition 3 (a) false as stated and its reading overstated, the example of Remark 3 false, and eleven smaller points; all were corrected in the theory note, the code's docstrings, the tests and this part (iteration 5 of `docs/iterations/E24.md`). No experiment was rerun and no number in the tables changed.

Binance spot one-minute bars, BTCUSDT, ETHUSDT, SOLUSDT, exactly as read by E22 (2024 to 2025) and E23 (2026, to 24 October 23:59 UTC); E19's calm-day pool (BTC, July to December 2025) for two synthetic designs; E6's sources and periods (five Binance coins and Bitstamp BTC, through E6's `prepare`) for the E19 diagnostic. No file after 24 October 2026 was read.
