## E25. An anytime-valid version of the forward release test: an e-process over releases

Pre-registration `docs/preregistration_e25_sequential.md` (commit `30804bb`, 3 November 2026, before any Binance return after 24 October 2026 23:59 UTC was loaded and before any code for this test was written), with **Amendment 1** (committed at 10:40 UTC on 3 November 2026, commit `e00c2b0`, before any fresh data) and **Amendment 2** (after review round 11, before any fresh data: refusals, a ledger and corrections; no rule, e-value or threshold changed) at its end; proof `docs/theory_sequential_events.md`; script `experiments/e25_sequential_events.py` (parts `theory`, `strata`, `gates`, `power`, `posthoc`, `status`, `dryrun`, `figs`; `--rules=original` reruns the rules as first committed); outputs `results/e25_*.csv` (amended rules) and `results/e25_*_original_rules.csv` (original rules, for comparison), figures `results/figures/e25_*.png`; tests `tests/test_e25.py` [SYNTHETIC]; iteration notes `docs/iterations/E25.md`. Labels: [PROVED], [SYNTHETIC], [REAL]. Every real-data result here is either a gate on known data or **post hoc and exploratory**: no fresh stratum is complete yet, and the fresh test has not been run.

**Question.** E24's forward test F24a is a fixed-sample test: it may be run once, on 1 June 2027, nobody may act on the data before then, and its sample cannot be extended after a failure without spending more than its 5%. Can the same question (do the rank monitor's up alarms come more often within six hours of FOMC statements and CPI releases than at matched control times?) be asked with a test that may be checked after every release and continued without an end date, at level 5% for every look; what does that cost in power; and what does it do on releases already seen?

**Design** (fixed in the pre-registration and Amendments 1 and 2; implemented without change). Each release i, in order of release time, gets a stratum: its own window [t, t + 6 h) and up to eight control windows at the same US Eastern weekday and clock time 1 to 4 weeks before and after it, chosen from the calendar only (rule 1); a candidate is dropped if its day is less than 2 days from a release day, if it is earlier than the stream start plus 1440 + 360 minutes, or if its window is not inside the data (rule 2), or if an earlier release already kept it or (Amendment 1) its window overlaps the window of any release or of any control already kept for an earlier release (rule 3); release windows are never dropped, and two that overlap are reported. A stratum enters the test when the data reach t + 28 days + 6 hours and no event-file row within 30 days still says "scheduled" (rule 4), and strata enter in order. Amendment 2 adds refusals to the status part only: a stratum is also not complete while the event file within 30 days of its windows lacks a CPI row for some month, lacks a row for a scheduled FOMC meeting, or has a `released` row whose access date precedes its date; and every reported stratum is kept in a ledger (`results/e25_status_ledger.csv`), so that a later look which computes any of them differently refuses and writes nothing. With Z_i the release window's outcome (an up alarm of S2, E14's awake rank monitor as in F24a), n_i controls kept, S_i windows with the outcome and p_i = S_i/(n_i + 1), the e-value is e_i(ψ) = ψ^{Z_i}/(1 - p_i + ψ p_i) and the e-process is M_j = (1/4) Σ_{ψ ∈ {2,4,8,16}} Π_{i≤j} e_i(ψ). Under H0 (the n_i + 1 outcomes of each stratum are exchangeable given the earlier strata), M is a nonnegative martingale with mean 1, so P(M_j ≥ 20 for some j) ≤ 5% whenever anyone looks and whatever stopping rule is used (Theorem 1 of the theory note, by Ville's inequality). Primary E25a: BTC, FOMC and CPI pooled, reject at the first complete stratum with M ≥ 20. Secondary E25b: ETH and SOL, M ≥ 40 each. F24a runs on 1 June 2027 unchanged; if either test is used to call the contrast confirmed, the report must say that two pre-registered 5% tests were run on the same releases (at most 10% together).

**Summary.**
* **Every gate passes.** [PROVED, checked exactly] The conditional mean of e(ψ) under H0 is exactly 1 in all 216 cases (n = 0 to 8, every S, every ψ of the grid; rational arithmetic). [REAL, known data] S2's alarms before each of four cut-offs (one of them at 14:37 UTC, inside a CPI window) are identical whether or not later data exist; E25's code reproduces the committed S2 alarms and the release outcomes of E22 and E23 exactly (34 checks, 0 mismatches). [SYNTHETIC] Under H0 the chance that M ever reaches 20 within 200 releases is at most 4.4% in every law (2.5% to 4.4% in the seven laws in which a stratum can carry evidence; 0 in the all-or-nothing law, where every e-value is 1; limit 5.46%).
* **Amendment 1 made the windows disjoint and costs controls.** [calendar only] On the planned calendar to December 2027 no two windows of different strata overlap any more (30 pairs under the original rules), and 95 of 184 candidates are kept (125 before): n_i ranges from 0 to 8, 5 of the 23 strata are balanced (as many kept controls before the release as after, at least one each side), 10 have controls on one side only and one (the FOMC statement of 17 March 2027) has none.
* **The fresh test cannot be computed yet.** Its first stratum, the FOMC statement of 28 October 2026 with 3 controls (4, 18 and 25 November 2026), completes on 26 November 2026 at 01:00 UTC, unchanged by the amendment; the status part refuses before any download until then, and was not run.
* **Power: less than F24a on 1 June 2027; E25's crossing probability passes F24a's power on 1 June 2027 (F24a's only date) between January and April 2028.** [SYNTHETIC; planning inputs REAL] At the pooled 2024 to 2026 planning rates M reaches 20 by 1 June 2027 with probability 0.43 (F24a: 0.82), by 1 January 2028 with 0.82, by 1 January 2029 with 0.98; at the 2026 rates 0.19, 0.51, 0.81 (F24a: 0.60); at half the pooled excess 0.13, 0.29, 0.52 (F24a: 0.37); under the null 0.010, 0.016, 0.022. The original rules gave 0.54, 0.89, 0.99 at the planning rates: disjoint windows cost about a fifth of the power at F24a's date.
* **Post hoc, on seen data** [REAL, exploratory]: on 2024 to 2025, M crosses 20 on BTC at the 8th of 36 strata (12 June 2024) and ends at 4.8 × 10⁴; on 2026, BTC's M ends at 3.8 after 15 strata and never reaches 20 (ETH 8.4, SOL 5.0).

### Amendment 1: what changed, when and why

The implementation of the rules as first committed (commits `d0c2d8f` to `80ee004`) found that rule 3 forbids a window being used twice but not two windows overlapping in time (a CPI control at 08:30 ET and an FOMC control at 14:00 ET on the same day share the half hour from 14:00 to 14:30 ET; 30 such pairs on the planned calendar), and that section 6's sentence on drift holds only for strata whose kept controls are balanced around the release. Both findings were reported, and the coordinator adopted them as Amendment 1 (rule 3 extended as above; the drift sentence restricted to balanced strata and the number of balanced strata reported; section 9's reference to "rule 4's assignment" corrected to rules 1 to 3).

**Order of events.** The amendment was committed at 10:40 UTC on 3 November 2026 (commit time of `e00c2b0`; its heading says about 10:50, which Amendment 2 corrects), one minute after the report part with the original-rule results (`80ee004`) and fifteen minutes before the amended rerun (`42207d0`). It was written after the synthetic power simulation (section 9) and after the post hoc run on seen data (section 10) had been done with the original rules, and before any Binance return after 24 October 2026 23:59 UTC was downloaded or loaded, so before any data of the fresh test. Its stated motivation is the logic of section 6 (an alarm in shared minutes would count in two strata, and a later stratum's control outcome would be partly known from an earlier one), not those results. A reader can check the direction: the amended rules lower both the simulated power and the post hoc values (table below), so the change did not favour the test. Every figure in this report uses the amended rules unless it says otherwise; the original-rule runs are kept in `results/e25_*_original_rules.csv` and compared in one table below. The status part (the fresh test) uses the amended rules only.

Gate 5 in detail (shares of 20,000 sequences of 200 strata on which M ever reaches the level; amended strata sizes):

| Law of the strata under H0 | ≥ 10 (bound 0.10) | ≥ 20 (bound 0.05) | ≥ 100 (bound 0.01) |
|---|---|---|---|
| n_i + 1 i.i.d. Bernoulli(5%) windows, release one of them at random | 0.057 | 0.025 | 0.004 |
| the same at 10% | 0.062 | 0.030 | 0.006 |
| the same at 20% | 0.065 | 0.031 | 0.006 |
| the same at 40% | 0.072 | 0.036 | 0.007 |
| all or nothing (S = 0 or n + 1): every e-value is 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| exactly one window with the outcome, at a uniform position | 0.063 | 0.031 | 0.006 |
| S uniform on 0..n + 1, release position uniform | 0.070 | 0.035 | 0.006 |
| S chosen from the earlier strata (1 after a release without the outcome, n after one with it) | 0.077 | 0.044 | 0.008 |

The bound is not attained by these laws, because M overshoots the threshold at the stratum where it crosses; the last law, in which S depends on the past (allowed by H0, which needs no independence between strata), comes closest. The mean of M after 1 and after 10 strata is 1 within two Monte Carlo standard errors in every law; after 200 strata the sample mean is below 1 in most laws, as expected for a test martingale whose mean is carried by rare very large values.

### The strata of the planned calendar (`e25_strata_planned.csv`)

The forward event file's released and scheduled rows (scheduled treated as released, for planning only) without the statement of 27 January 2027, stream start 25 October 2026 00:00 UTC, no data end: 23 strata to December 2027 (8 FOMC, 15 CPI). 95 of 184 candidates are kept. Rule 2 drops 6 candidates before the stream start plus 1800 minutes and 37 within 2 days of a release; rule 3 drops 14 already used by an earlier release (two each from seven strata) and, under Amendment 1, 32 whose windows overlap a control window already kept for an earlier release (none overlaps a release window on this calendar, and no two release windows overlap). The mechanism is the Wednesday: CPI releases (08:30 ET) and FOMC statements (14:00 ET) often fall on Wednesdays within four weeks of each other, and the earlier one's Wednesday controls, [08:30, 14:30) or [14:00, 20:00) ET, overlap the later one's Wednesday candidates by 30 minutes. The FOMC statement of 17 March 2027 loses all eight candidates (six to the controls of the CPI release of 10 March 2027, two to rule 2) and enters with n = 0, so its e-value is 1 whatever happens; the CPI releases of 12 May and 10 November 2027 keep one control each.

| | n_i = 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | balanced | one side only |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| amended rules (23 strata to December 2027) | 1 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 5 | 3 | 2 | 1 | 3 | 5 | 10 |
| amended rules, with F24a's 2028 placeholders (41 strata to January 2029) | 1 | 4 | 6 | 5 | 9 | 4 | 4 | 3 | 5 | 8 | 19 |

Balanced means as many kept controls before the release as after it and at least one on each side (Amendment 1, item 2); the five balanced strata are the CPI releases of 10 December 2026, 11 February, 10 March, 14 September and 10 December 2027. In the other 17 strata with controls, a linear drift is not removed to first order, and the imbalance is systematic, not random: strata are filled in release order and each takes its later candidates before the next release can, so every one-sided stratum has its controls after the release (10 of 10 to December 2027, 19 of 19 with the 2028 placeholders), and the planned strata keep 31 controls before their releases against 64 after (57 against 115 to January 2029). A falling alarm rate therefore favours rejection and a rising one works against it. The effect on the level is small for plausible drifts: with no release effect and every window's rate halving every 91 days, M ever reaches 20 over the 41 planned strata with probability 0.0258 against 0.0226 without drift (s.e. 0.0011; reviewer's simulation, `docs/review/round11_scripts/r11_drift_sim.py`) [SYNTHETIC]. This is part of what H0 assumes away (Amendment 2, item 3).

Eastern day arithmetic follows the clock across daylight saving changes: the controls of the CPI release of 10 March 2027 are at 13:30 UTC before 14 March and 12:30 UTC after. The first stratum (FOMC, 28 October 2026, 18:00 UTC) keeps 4, 18 and 25 November 2026 at 14:00 EST, as under the original rules (its earlier candidates precede the stream; 11 November is one day from the CPI release of 10 November) and completes when the data reach 25 November 2026 20:00 EST (four weeks after the release, plus 6 hours), that is **26 November 2026, 01:00 UTC**, provided the event file's row for the CPI release of 10 November 2026 has been updated by then. **Releases on consecutive days.** H0 needs no independence between strata, but it does need the earlier strata to carry no information that separates a release window from its controls. Every control is at least 2 days from every release, while releases are not kept apart from each other: 4 pairs of releases are one or two days apart to December 2027 (9 and 10 December 2026, 9 and 10 June 2027, 14 and 15 September 2027, 8 and 10 December 2027; 7 pairs to January 2029). The monitor's state after the first release carries into the second release's window but not into its controls, so any short-range dependence of S2's alarms can separate them. On seen data the one-day dependence is weak and, where it can be measured, mostly negative, the conservative direction (odds ratio of an up alarm in the 08:30 ET window given one in the 14:00 ET window the day before: BTC 0.75, ETH 0.62, SOL 0.63; 14:00 ET given 08:30 ET the day before: BTC 0.16, ETH 1.63, SOL 0.82; 383 release-free day pairs per coin; reviewer's `r11_lag_dependence.py`) [REAL, seen data, descriptive].

**Holiday controls.** 6 of the 95 planned controls fall on US holidays or their eves, all in the two December CPI strata, which are two of the five balanced ones: Thanksgiving (26 November 2026) and the day after it (26 November 2027), and 24 and 31 December of both years (in 2027 these are also the observed federal holidays for Christmas and New Year's Day); a seventh, 25 November 2026 in the first stratum, is the day before Thanksgiving. Holiday trading can move the alarm rate either way; this, too, is part of what H0 assumes away.

With the 2028 placeholders of F24a's plan, 41 strata enter by early January 2029 (`e25_power_calendar.csv`).

### Power (pre-registration, section 9) [SYNTHETIC; planning inputs REAL] (`e25_power.csv`, `e25_power_growth.csv`, figure `e25_power.png`)

F24a's planning model: the release window has the outcome with S2's BTC rate of its type, each control with the matched control rate of its type, all independently (pooled 2024 to 2026: FOMC 77.3% against 16.5%, CPI 37.5% against 12.5%; `results/e24_future_planning_inputs.csv`). Strata from E25's amended rules on F24a's planning calendar; a stratum enters when complete, assuming each event-file row is updated when its release happens. 10 strata enter by 1 June 2027 (F24a counts 11 releases: the CPI release of 12 May 2027 is in F24a's sample, but its stratum completes on 10 June), 21 by 1 January 2028, 39 by 1 January 2029. Seed 25,000; 20,000 replications per scenario (Monte Carlo s.e. at most 0.0035).

| Scenario | F24a, power on 1 June 2027 | E25: P(M ≥ 20) by 1 June 2027 | by 1 January 2028 | by 1 January 2029 | median releases to the crossing | oracle that knows the control rate, by the same three dates |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| pooled 2024 to 2026 (planning) | 0.822 | 0.435 | 0.820 | 0.981 | 12 | 0.753, 0.957, 0.998 |
| 2026 rates only | 0.596 | 0.194 | 0.509 | 0.809 | 20 (18 among those that cross by 2029) | 0.409, 0.786, 0.953 |
| half of the pooled excess | 0.369 | 0.127 | 0.295 | 0.516 | 38 (19 among those that cross by 2029) | 0.268, 0.452, 0.669 |
| null (release rate = control rate) | 0.031 | 0.010 | 0.016 | 0.022 | never in 97.8% | 0.018, 0.022, 0.025 |

(F24a's values are those of `results/e24_future_power.csv`, S2 pooled; the script checks them. The oracle's e-value does not depend on n_i, so its column is the same under both rule sets.) Estimating each stratum's control rate from at most 8 controls lowers the crossing probability on 1 June 2027 by 42% to 53% relative to the oracle (29% to 40% under the original rules). The expected log e-value per release, exact under the model, is largest at ψ = 8 under the pooled rates (0.26 per release; 0.53 for an FOMC statement, 0.11 for a CPI release) and at ψ = 4 under the 2026 rates (0.14; a CPI release contributes −0.005) and at half the excess (0.074). If only the best ψ contributed, M ≥ 20 would need that ψ's product to reach 80 (the average over four ψ pays a factor 4), a log growth of 4.4, that is about 17 releases at the mean growth of the pooled rates; the simulated median, 12, is earlier because the other products also contribute and the path fluctuates.

So at F24a's date E25 has about half of F24a's power at the planning rates and about a third at the smaller effects; its crossing probability passes F24a's power on 1 June 2027 on 6 January 2028 at the planning rates (0.855), on 10 February 2028 at the 2026 rates (0.601) and on 5 April 2028 at half the excess (0.371) (`e25_power_curve.csv`), and it is the only one of the two that can continue. (F24a has a single power, at its only date; the comparison is between E25's crossing probability at later dates and that one number. The figure's dates assume that the event file is updated at each release and, for the strata from 10 November 2027 on, that the 2028 FOMC schedule has been added, which Amendment 2's check requires.)

The strata without controls are FOMC statements one week after a Wednesday CPI release or on its day (12 June 2024, which shares its day with a CPI release; 18 December 2024; 18 June 2025; 17 June 2026). No control window shares a minute with a window of another stratum, but two release windows can: those of the CPI release and the FOMC statement of 12 June 2024 overlap by 30 minutes, the only such pair in either period. Both enter, as Amendment 1 requires, and the overlap is harmless here because the later stratum, the FOMC statement, loses its Wednesday candidates to the CPI release's controls and enters with n = 0 (e = 1); by rules 2 and 3 this happens to every same-day pair away from the first 30 hours of the stream. On 2024 to 2025 the procedure would have crossed at a release of June to August 2024 on every coin (the crossing is known when that stratum completes, four weeks after the release). On 2026, BTC's M fell to 0.28 by mid February 2026 and stayed there until the FOMC statement of 29 April (the first release with an alarm), recovered with the releases of July to September, and ended at 3.8; BTC's FOMC statements alone (exploratory) end at 7.7, CPI releases alone at 0.66. E23's fixed-sample stratified test of the same S2 BTC releases (a secondary family) gave p = 0.007 with 29 to 39 controls per release; with at most 8 controls (median 4) and Ville's threshold the e-process does not reach 20 on the same evidence, which is the cost the power section describes.

Three exploratory checks asked for by review round 11 (`e25_posthoc_summary.csv`). *Control rates before and after the release* (m2): on 2024 to 2025 the controls before their releases had the outcome more often than those after (BTC 5 of 34, 14.7%, against 10 of 85, 11.8%; ETH 17.6% against 11.8%; SOL 17.6% against 10.6%), the direction that favours rejection; on 2026 the opposite (BTC 1 of 24, 4.2%, against 6 of 42, 14.3%; ETH and SOL 4.2% against 19.0%). The two groups come from different strata, so these are descriptions, not a test of drift. *M over the balanced strata alone*: 3 strata in each period, final M 0.35, 0.51, 0.30 (BTC, ETH, SOL) on 2024 to 2025 and 1.61, 0.97, 1.46 on 2026 (under the original rules, 8 and 4 balanced strata: 1.68, 0.84, 0.72 and 0.97, 0.65, 0.90). *Missing minutes inside windows* (m10): none in any release or control window of either period on any coin (0 of 155 windows per coin in 2024 to 2025 and 0 of 81 in 2026); the status part now reports this count per stratum at every look.

### What E25 shows and what it does not

* It shows [PROVED; checked exactly and by simulation] that the pre-registered e-process has the guarantee claimed: under H0 the chance that it ever reaches 20 is at most 5%, for any number of looks and releases; in the simulated laws it is at most 4.4% within 200 releases (2.5% to 4.4% in the seven laws in which a stratum can carry evidence, 0 in the all-or-nothing law). The guarantee does not depend on the strata rules; Amendment 1 strengthens the case for H0, not the proof: no control window shares a minute with a window of another stratum, while two release windows can (12 June 2024), and the later stratum then has no controls.
* It shows [REAL, known data] that the pipeline that will compute it is causal and reproduces E22's and E23's committed outcomes exactly.
* It shows [SYNTHETIC] that the price of looking at any time is power at a fixed date (0.43 against F24a's 0.82 on 1 June 2027 at the planning rates) and that the gain is the ability to continue (0.82 by 2028, 0.98 by 2029): E25's crossing probability at later dates exceeds F24a's power at its only date from January to April 2028, depending on the effect. The price of disjoint windows is about 0.1 of the power on 1 June 2027.
* It does **not** yet test anything on fresh data: the first fresh stratum completes on 26 November 2026. The post hoc paths are illustrations on seen data.
* A crossing would say that release windows differ from their controls under this monitor; it would not say which release type carries the effect, how large it is (M is not an effect size), or that the monitor's own 5% bound holds on these data (it does not; E22, E23).

### Caveats and what failed

* Amendment 1 was made after the synthetic power and the post hoc run on seen data had been seen (order of events above). It lowered both; the original-rule results are kept in full.
* Under the amended rules most strata are unbalanced (of the 22 planned strata with controls, 10 have them on one side only, all after the release, and 7 more on both sides in unequal numbers), so H0's exchangeability within a stratum carries more of the weight against slow drift than section 6 first claimed, and a falling alarm rate favours rejection (strata section). An earlier version of this part counted 4 balanced strata under the original rules using a stricter criterion (mean offset of the controls from the release equal to zero); the amendment's criterion (equal numbers before and after) gives 6 under the original rules and 5 under the amended ones.
* Wednesday releases lose the most controls: the FOMC statement of 17 March 2027 has none, and so do four of the seen FOMC statements. A stratum without controls contributes e = 1 and only delays the test.
* The planning entry times assume that the event file is updated at each release; a later update delays strata, never changes them. Amendment 2's check also keeps the strata from 10 November 2027 on out of the test until the 2028 FOMC schedule is added to the schedule list the check reads (`E24.FUTURE_FOMC_SCHEDULED`, which ends in December 2027).
* Releases one or two days apart, holiday controls and the systematic placement of controls after the release are three ways in which H0 could fail without the proof failing (strata section); none is tested by the gates.
* The mean of M after 200 simulated strata was first reported as a validity check and replaced by the means after 1 and 10 strata (a test martingale's sample mean over long horizons is dominated by rare values).
* A test of the status refusal assumed that complete data make a stratum complete; the code was right (a scheduled row within 30 days also blocks), the test was corrected. An empty release list broke a pandas mask; fixed (iteration 1).
* E12's `alarm_frame` prints division-by-zero warnings for S2 alarms with a zero baseline scale, in a diagnostic column that E25 does not use.
* The official schedule hosts cannot be fetched from this machine; the forward calendar rests on E24's event file, verified through search results that index the official pages.

## TH4. Robustness of the guarantee: how much can a small drift of the conditional mean inflate the false alarm probability?

Theory `docs/theory_robustness.md` (statements, proofs and the full tables); code `src/avmonitor/robustness.py`; script `experiments/th4_robustness.py`; outputs `results/th4_*.csv` and `results/figures/th4_sup_bound.png`, `results/figures/th4_e16_comparison.png`; tests `tests/test_robustness.py`; iteration notes `docs/iterations/TH4.md`. The theorems are proved in the theory note; all numerical results are **[SYNTHETIC]**, with seeds fixed in the script.

**Question.** Theorem B proves `P(false alarm within m steps) ≤ m / A` for the default two-sided detector when the conditional mean of the clipped squared return is exactly the baseline m0. E16 mapped where the bound fails when that condition fails: GARCH clustering, a plug-in baseline, price ticks. What can be proved when the condition holds only approximately, `E[X_t | past] ≤ m0 (1 + δ_t)` on the increase side and `≥ m0 (1 - δ_t)` on the decrease side? How fast does the guarantee degrade with the drift δ? Which forms of drift are harmless? What does the plug-in baseline cost? And how do the bounds compare with E16's measured rates?

**Set-up.** The default detector of Theorem B: six increase bets λ = 0.02 to 0.5, five decrease bets 0.1 to 0.95 times 1 / (B - 1), Shiryaev-Roberts statistics, each side alarming at 2A, A = 7800, so the bound is 5% for one 390-step day and 25% for five days. The drift `δ_t ≥ 0` may change over time but must be known one step ahead. Its smallest values are the positive and negative parts of `E[X_t | past] / m0 - 1`.

**Summary.**
* **A bounded drift inflates the bound by a closed-form factor (Theorem 1, proved).** If the drift never exceeds δ, then `P(T ≤ m) ≤ (m / A) I_m(δ)` with `I_m(δ) = ½ [Σ_k w_k G_m(λ_k δ↑) + Σ_l v_l G_m(φ_l δ↓)]` and `G_m(x) = (1 + x) ((1 + x)^m - 1) / (m x)`. The factor is about `1 + (m + 1)(λ̄ δ↑ + φ̄ δ↓) / 4` while `λ_max δ m` is small. Once `λ_max δ m` is large it grows like `(1 + λ_max δ)^m`. At one day a drift of 0.1% on both sides gives 5.14% instead of 5%, 0.5% gives 5.80% and 1% gives 7.06%. **Design guide:** the one-day bound reaches 10% at a drift of 1.63% and 25% at 2.66% (upward drift only, a mean between m0 and `m0 (1 + δ)`: 1.72% and 2.70%; downward drift only: 6.36% and 10.51%). Over five days a drift of 0.5% on both sides, or upward, already gives 1. The bound cannot be lowered where it reaches 1, because a deterministic stream at `m0 (1 + δ)` attains it at its alarm step. Below that, in one day, the strongest adaptive stream found reaches 0.33 to 0.63 of it, and whether the bound is attained there is open.
* **A drift that averages out is cheap, but only a pathwise bound can see it (Theorems 2 and 3, proved).** What matters is the largest product of `(1 + bet × drift)` over a window. A calm spell resets it. For any drift known one step ahead (Theorem 2), `P(T ≤ m) ≤ K m / A + P(max window product > K)`. When the drift does not respond to the data (Theorem 3, with the largest window product over the whole horizon) the bound is the detector run on the drift itself. For a ±10% switching drift that flips at every step, Theorem 3 gives 15.3% at one day, where the sup form gives 1 (measured 0.73%). **What cannot be said:** when the drift responds to the data, Theorem 3's formula is not a bound (a stream where it gives 10.2% at one day against an alarm probability of 11.1%). No bound of the form `C(mean drift) × m / A` exists (a seven-step burst decided before monitoring). A bound in the mean drift exists (Proposition 4), but its extra term is weighted by A and is larger than the whole one-day budget once the mean upward drift exceeds 0.026%.
* **Plug-in baseline (Corollary 1, proved).** The baseline error is a drift fixed by the calibration window, so `P(T ≤ m) ≤ E_W[min{1, (m / A) I_m(δ(W))}]`. For Gaussian returns and 390 calibration steps this is 41.8% at one day and 92.4% at five days. E16 measured 4.0% and 41.8% for i.i.d. returns, and 32.5% and 85.8% for its noise-free shape adversary, so the bound is within a factor of 1.3 of that stream. The one-day bound is 7.3% at 11,520 calibration steps and 6.0% at 23,040. This is consistent with Proposition A.6 (E14): the constant in front of m / A has to grow with m.
* **Against E16, every proved bound is above every measured rate where its assumption holds.** That covers 128 GARCH cells, 36 plug-in cells and 80 decile cells, plus 112 new constant-drift and switching cells. For GARCH the sup form gives 1 everywhere, because the conditional mean comes arbitrarily close to `B m0`. The proved pathwise bound is informative in 22 of 64 cells at one day (6 to 29 times the measured rate) and 6 at five days, all with a small drift. Theorem 3 used as a heuristic is 1.2 to 8.3 times the measured rate and was never below it.

**Tightness** (`results/th4_constant_drift.csv`, `results/th4_sharpness.csv`, figure `th4_sup_bound.png`). The setting is 80 cells with a known constant drift, 10,000 paths per i.i.d. law and 20,000 for the adaptive stream. The adaptive stream holds Y at its mean for a searched number of steps, then plays bold as in E16. No rate is above the bound. The deterministic stream alarms within one day from an upward drift of 3.756%, and the bound reaches 1 at 3.740%, so Theorem 1 is attained where it reaches 1. Below that drift the deterministic stream does not alarm within the day (at the 10% and 25% design drifts it alarms at steps 515 to 795), the adaptive stream is the strongest found, and the worst case is open. At an upward drift of 2% it gives 6.6% in one day against a bound of 12.4%, and at 3% it gives 22.7% against 35.9%. Noisy i.i.d. streams barely notice a small drift within a day: the two-point law {0, B} gives 2.0% at a drift of 0.25% and 2.4% at 5%.

The five-day bound is 92.4% down to 57.7%. (The 390-step value, 42.1% on 20,000 windows, is the 41.8% of the table on other windows.)

### Reading

The guarantee of Theorem B degrades smoothly, not abruptly. A drift of the conditional mean of a few tenths of a percent costs a few percent of the bound over a day. The cost then compounds: the one-day bound doubles at a drift of about 1.6% and reaches 1 at about 3.7% (upward drift). Over five days a drift of 0.5% exhausts it. This gives a concrete scale for "the null holds approximately". Where the bound reaches 1 the scale is sharp: a deterministic stream at m0 (1 + δ) alarms within the day from an upward drift of 3.756%, where the bound reaches 1 at 3.740%. At the design drifts the deterministic stream does not alarm within the day, the strongest stream found reaches 0.33 to 0.63 of the bound, and whether the 10% and 25% values are attained is open. For noisy streams it is conservative: with a constant upward drift of 2%, i.i.d. Gaussian returns alarm on 1.5% of days and the two-point law {0, B} on 1.9%, against a bound of 12.4%. Drift that alternates is far cheaper than its size suggests, but only a pathwise bound can show it. When the drift responds to the data, as under GARCH, the proved pathwise bound has to cover the case where a high drift comes exactly when the wealth is high, which makes it loose. The plug-in baseline is a persistent drift fixed before monitoring starts, the case where nothing averages out, and there Corollary 1 is close to the worst stream E16 found. In practice the drift must be kept small and short-lived relative to the baseline. That is what E8 (a confidence-sequence baseline), E10 (a forecast-relative null) and E14 (a rank detector) are for.

### Caveats

* The proved bounds are statements about all streams with a given drift. Their numerical values for GARCH, switching and the plug-in are Monte Carlo estimates of expectations over the drift, and the threshold K of Theorem 2 is chosen on the same paths (optimistic by at most 1.75 points with 95% probability, by the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz inequality; adding this changes no count).
* Theorem 3 for GARCH and Theorem 1 at E16's mean drift are heuristics. They held in every cell here, but neither is a bound in general: section 3.4 of the theory note gives, for each, a stream with a drift that responds to the data or is decided before monitoring where it is below the alarm probability at one day.
* Price ticks are not covered. The theorems need the drift given the whole past, which for rounded prices is a filtering problem, and E16 stored the drift given the previous return only. Theorem 1 at that drift (`results/th4_ticks.csv`) is a heuristic that can be too small.
* The worst case over streams with a given constant drift, at horizons shorter than the deterministic alarm step, is not known. The adaptive stream is a lower bound on it.
* All statements are for band 0. With the monitor's null band b, Theorem 1 holds with the drifts reduced to `((δ↑ - b) / (1 + b))⁺` and `((δ↓ - b) / (1 - b))⁺` (remark after Theorem 1 in the theory note).
* Everything is synthetic and for the default grid with A = 7800 (one design row uses A = 28,800).

## TH5. Limits for every valid procedure, and the plug-in baseline when n, m and A grow together

Theory `docs/theory_limits.md` (statements, proofs and the full tables); code `src/avmonitor/limits.py`; script `experiments/th5_limits.py`; outputs `results/th5_*.csv` and `results/figures/th5_floors.png`, `results/figures/th5_plugin_regime.png`; tests `tests/test_limits.py`; iteration notes `docs/iterations/TH5.md`. The theorems are proved in the theory note; all numerical results are **[SYNTHETIC]**, with seeds fixed in the script.

**Question.** Sections 2, 3 and M3 of the referee report. (1) The decrease speed limit of `docs/theory_delay.md` (58 steps on a complete collapse for any Shiryaev-Roberts e-detector with linear bets at c = 3, A = 7800) is a statement about e-detectors. How fast can *any* procedure with the guarantee of Theorem B detect a change, and how far are the e-detectors from that? (2) When does the plug-in baseline keep the nominal false alarm level if the calibration length n, the horizon m and the alarm level A grow together, and what margin restores it? (3) Why is the growth-optimal decrease bet so close to its upper limit `λ_max = 1 / (B - 1)`?

**Set-up.** Monitored statistic `Y = min(r², τ²) / m₀ ∈ [0, B]`, nonparametric null classes (conditional mean of Y at least 1, at most 1, or equal to 1; laws need not be independent or identical), validity `P(T ≤ n) ≤ n / A` for every n (Theorem B). Default detector: six increase bets, five decrease bets, each side at 2A, A = 7800, c = 3. Post-change laws for delays: Gaussian, Student t3 and the jump law of E4, sd ratios 0.5, 0.67, 0.8, 1.25, 1.5 and 2, change at the first step, true baseline. Plug-in: Gaussian and Student t3 returns, n = 390 to 92,160, m = 98 to 7800.

**Summary.**
* **A speed limit for every valid procedure (Theorem 2, proved).** On a path y, a rule valid at levels `n / A` can stop at step n only if `W_n(y) = Π_{s ≤ n} 1 / π(y_s) ≥ A / n`, where `π(y)` is the largest probability a null law can put on the value y: `(B - 1) / (B - y)` for `y < 1` (decreases), `1 / y` for `y > 1` (increases). The proof places an independent two-point null law at each step, under which the path has probability exactly `1 / W_n(y)`. The floor is exact path by path, holds for rules that see the raw returns, and a randomised rule can beat it only with probability at most `(n / A) W_n(y)`.
* **Complete collapse: 45 steps for every deterministic procedure (Corollary 4, proved).** With all returns zero at c = 3 (B = 9.045), no deterministic valid procedure alarms before step 45 at A = 7800 (50 at 2A), against 57.7 for every Shiryaev-Roberts e-detector with linear bets and 73 for the default grid (79 at 2A). A randomised valid procedure can alarm by step n on this path with probability at most `min(1, n W_n / A)` (0.98 at step 44), and its mean delay there is at least 43.4 (48.5 at 2A; a linear programme). The 13 steps between 45 and 58 are the factor `n / B` in the level that one path allows and an e-detector, which must spread `E M_n ≤ n` over all paths, cannot use. At c = 2 the numbers are 23, 28.7 and 36. Without truncation no deterministic valid procedure alarms before step A on any path (a randomised one by step n < A with probability at most n / A), the sequential form of `docs/math.md` 5.3.
* **The e-detectors are within a factor of about 2 of the best possible delay (Theorem 5, proved; numbers Monte Carlo).** Combining the pathwise floor with a Neyman-Pearson bound at the least favourable null law gives a lower bound on the mean delay of every valid deterministic procedure. Over the 18 laws, one detector side at level A takes 1.69 to 2.16 times the bound (default grid) and 1.34 to 1.76 times (growth-optimal single bet); against the bound for randomised procedures, 1.81 to 2.24 and 1.53 to 1.80. These ratios bound the inefficiency from above, since no rule is known to attain the bound. As a consistency check of the code, no alarm of either, on 180,000 paths at two levels, came before the pathwise floor.
* **The plug-in keeps its level exactly when m is small compared with √n (Theorem 8, Corollary 10, proved).** The drift of the plug-in baseline is at most `B̂ D_n`, with `D_n` the Kolmogorov distance between the window and the return law. So, for every stream in the class `C(W)` of streams whose conditional truncated mean at τ̂ equals that of the return law, `P(T ≤ m) ≤ (m / A)(1 + C (m + 1) / √n (1 + o(1)))` when `m / √n → 0`, with `C = 0.037` for Gaussian and 0.047 for Student t3 returns (first order) and `C = 1.79` for every law. Conversely, a stream in `C(W)` that holds the drift and then bets boldly makes `P(T ≤ m) / (m / A) → ∞` when `m / √n → ∞`, `m / log A → ∞` and `m / A → 0`. The boundary is `m ≍ √n` for any A with `log A = o(m)`. At one day after a 390-step window of Gaussian returns, the largest false alarm probability over `C(W)` is at least about 33% and at most about 42% (nominal 5%): these are window averages of proved per-window bounds, estimated by Monte Carlo (32.3% and 41.6% over 20,000 windows in the CSV; 32.3% to 33.2% and 41.6% to 42.2% over six runs of 20,000 windows; standard errors 0.33 and 0.30 points). The hold-then-bold stream, simulated, gives 36.5%. For i.i.d. monitored returns the excess is much smaller and falls quickly with n (simulated, Q-TH5c).
* **The margin for the plug-in is the normal quantile (Proposition 11, proved).** Baselines `m̂ ± z se` keep `P(T ≤ m) ≤ m / A + 2 Φ̄(z) + o(1)` uniformly in m and A, and the worst stream attains `2 Φ̄(z)` when `m / (√n log A) → ∞`; so `z = Φ⁻¹(1 - δ / 2)`. The confidence-sequence baseline (Theorem D) guarantees the same without asymptotics at an effective z of 3.8 to 5.7.
* **The decrease optimum is at the boundary only for light tails (Proposition 12, proved).** The growth of the bet `λ_max (1 - ε)` is `G_c + q_B log ε` up to small terms, with `q_B` the probability that a return reaches the truncation level, and `ε* = q_B / h(ε*)`. For Gaussian halving `q_B = 2 × 10⁻⁹` and `ε* = 2.4 × 10⁻⁸`, the referee's value. For Student t3 `q_B` is 0.6% to 2.4% and `λ* / λ_max` is 0.93 to 0.55; a bet at `λ_max (1 - 10⁻⁶)` has negative growth there and is up to 53% slower.

* For i.i.d. returns the true baseline is itself well below nominal (0.85% to 1.64% at one day, 12.2% to 15.0% at five days), so the plug-in's excess appears first as a ratio to the true baseline. At five days that ratio is 3.4, 1.9, 1.5, 1.19, 1.13 and 1.07 for Gaussian returns as n goes from 390 to 23,040 (2.9 to 1.06 for t3), although `m / √n` is still 13 at n = 23,040. The worst stream in the class is much worse than i.i.d. returns; the comparison with the heuristic scale `log A / √n` of the theory note (section 4.6) was made after seeing the results [post hoc].
* The plug-in is not significantly above nominal at one day in any cell (largest 5.14% for t3 at n = 390, interval 4.72% to 5.59%), but it is far above at five days after a one-day window (40.8% and 42.3% against 25%).
* No simulated rate is above its Corollary 1 bound (all 288 rows). With z = 2.576 the inflated plug-in's bound is at most 1.061 times nominal in every cell, and the share of windows outside the shifted baselines is 0.009 to 0.013 against `2 Φ̄(2.576) = 0.01` (Proposition 11b). The inflated plug-in and the cs baseline are conservative for i.i.d. returns (at most 0.75% and 0.63% at one day); their price is a later alarm after a change, which TH5 does not measure.

Where the growth is negative the delay stays finite: the Shiryaev-Roberts statistic restarts after each return at the truncation level and alarms on a long enough run without one (Proposition 12e gives an ε-free bound, which is loose).

### Reading

The guarantee of Theorem B has a price that no procedure can avoid, and the e-detectors pay at most about twice the minimum. On the hardest path for the decrease side, a complete collapse, every deterministic procedure with the guarantee needs 45 steps at c = 3 (a randomised one at least 43.4 on average), the best e-detectors 58 and the default grid 73. Across realistic post-change laws one side of the default grid is at most 1.7 to 2.2 times slower than the best valid deterministic procedure could be on average (at most 1.8 to 2.2 against randomised ones), and the best single bet at most 1.3 to 1.8 times. These are upper bounds on the inefficiency, because the lower bound need not be attained. So at least half of the delay is the problem's, through the truncation level B, for the best single bet in all 18 laws and for the default grid in 16 of them (at least 46% in every law: the grid's ratio is 2.16 at Gaussian sd ratio 0.8 and 2.03 for jumps at 0.8); the rest is an unknown split between the detector and the slack in the bound.

For the plug-in baseline the relevant comparison is the horizon against the square root of the calibration length. For every stream in `C(W)`, the bound of Theorem B is inflated by at most `1 + C (m + 1) / √n` to first order when m is small compared with √n. The scale √n is sharp: for `m ≫ √n` (and `m ≫ log A`) some stream in `C(W)` breaks the nominal level by an unbounded factor. The constant C is not shown to be sharp. With minute data, a one-day horizon equals √n at n = 152,100 returns (390 trading days), which is the boundary itself, and is short compared with √n only for calibration windows of order 10⁶ returns or more. A margin of `z = Φ⁻¹(1 - δ / 2)` standard errors restores `m / A + δ` asymptotically, and the confidence-sequence baseline restores it exactly at a wider margin.

### Caveats

* The floors are for the change at the first step (no pre-change data), which is the worst case in Lorden's sense; they do not bound the conditional delay after a pre-change history (E4's delays, which used one, are smaller than E11's).
* The Neyman-Pearson parts of the delay bound are Monte Carlo estimates (importance weights from 10,000 paths per law), not certified values; batch-means standard errors are in `results/th5_floors.csv`. The pathwise floor is exact on each path.
* The delay floors of Q-TH5b are for one detector side and one-sided validity; the bound for the two-sided guarantee over `H=` is smaller and was not computed.
* The bounds concern rules valid over the full nonparametric null. A procedure valid only over a smaller model (for example a fixed return shape) is not covered.
* The plug-in lower bound uses an adversarial stream that knows the drift of the window. For i.i.d. monitored returns the boundary is not proved; a heuristic suggests the scale `log A / √n` (theory note, section 4.6), and the simulation of Q-TH5c shows a much smaller excess than the worst case.
* The distribution-free constant (1.79) is 48 times the Gaussian one (0.037); its bound is informative only for `m` well below `√n / 20`.
* Everything is synthetic and for the default grid with c = 3 and A = 7800, except where a table varies c or A.

## TH6. False alarms after the first day: what Theorem B bounds, and two detectors with a bound for every day (referee M2 and M4)

Theory `docs/theory_per_period.md` (statements, proofs and the full tables); `docs/math.md` (remark after Theorem B; Theorem 6.4 restated, which the referee report calls Theorem D); code `src/avmonitor/periodic.py` (closed-form bounds, a vectorised simulation engine, `PeriodicVolatilityMonitor`); script `experiments/th6_per_period.py`; outputs `results/th6_*.csv` and `results/figures/th6_hazard.png`, `results/figures/th6_delay.png`; tests `tests/test_periodic.py`; iteration notes `docs/iterations/TH6.md`. The propositions and theorems are proved in the theory note; all numerical results are **[SYNTHETIC]**, with seeds fixed in the script.

**Question.** (M2) Theorem B proves `P(T ≤ m) ≤ m / A` for the first false alarm T, and the paper and README read it as "at most 5% per day". What does it bound after the first day? How large is the probability of a false alarm on day d in practice? What detector gives a bound for every day, and at what cost in delay? How do these guarantees relate to the window-limited criteria of Lai (1998) and to Mei (2008)? (M4) Restate Theorem D with a null hypothesis that does not depend on the bets the algorithm chooses, and say what it excludes.

**Set-up.** The default two-sided detector with the true baseline: X = min(r², τ²), Y = X / m0 ∈ [0, B]; six increase bets 0.02 to 0.5 and five decrease bets 0.1 to 0.95 times 1 / (B - 1); each side the average of its bets, alarming at 2A. A = 7800 for 390-step days and 28,800 for 1440-step days (m / A = 5%). Twenty days. Streams: i.i.d. Gaussian, Student t3, jump and tick returns (the four laws of E9, with τ and m0 computed exactly, `results/th6_laws.csv`); the referee's stream (`|r| = √m0`, so Y = 1, for nine days, then Gaussian), and the referee's family (Y = 1 for d - 1 days, then one Gaussian or two-point day); E16's bold play run for 20 days. Detectors: the plain Shiryaev-Roberts (SR) detector; SR restarted at 0 at every day boundary; the CUSUM-type e-detector `C_t = f_t max(C_{t-1}, 1)` (e-CUSUM). With a restart after every alarm (a recalibration with the true baseline) we record the probability of at least one alarm on day d and the expected number of alarms per day; for the first alarm, `p_d = P(T on day d)` and the hazard `h_d = P(T on day d | T > (d - 1) m)`. 40,000 paths per stream (bold play and park and strike 30,000; delays 20,000 per cell).

**Summary.**
* **Theorem B is a bound for the first day after a (re)start, and no bound below 1 holds for all later days (Proposition 1, proved).** For day d it gives only `d m / A`, which no example reached (at most 35.7% against 50% at d = 10). The i.i.d. law Y = 1 is in the null and makes the default detector alarm with certainty on day 40. A remark after Theorem B in `docs/math.md` now says this, and the bullet "5% per trading day" there is corrected.
* **Measured.** For i.i.d. returns the hazard of the plain detector rises from 0.98% to 1.52% on day 1 to 4.60% to 4.70% on average over days 11 to 20 (390-step days); no single i.i.d. day is significantly above 5%. Bold play, which is inside the null class, averages 5.25% over days 11 to 20 (5.23% pooled over path-days, standard error about 0.06 points; the pooling over days 11 to 20 was chosen after seeing the results). For the referee's family the probability of a false alarm on day d is 11.3% at d = 5, 28.0% at d = 10 and 65.1% at d = 20. Corollary C held everywhere: 0.037 to 0.048 false alarms per day over 20 days, against 0.05.
* **Two detectors with a bound for every day (Theorems 1 and 2, proved).** (1) SR restarted at every day boundary, with a known baseline: at most m / A = 5% on every day, given everything before the day, under the martingale-difference null of Theorem B; `PeriodicVolatilityMonitor(period=m, baseline="known", tau=..., m0=...)` implements it exactly. With the confidence-sequence baseline the restart gives δ + m / A for each day of a segment, marginally and not given the past, while the tolerance of Theorem D holds to the end of that day (Corollary 1 of the theory note); with the plug-in baseline nothing per day is proved. Measured on every stream and day: the probability of a false alarm on a day was at most 2.66% (390) and 3.52% (1440), and the hazard at most 2.75% (390) and 3.52% (1440), all for bold play. (2) The e-CUSUM: by time reversal, `P(C_s ≥ x) ≤ 1 / x` at every s under an i.i.d. (or exchangeable) null with a known baseline and fixed bets, which gives at most `(m + log 2A + (log 6 + log 5) / 2) / A` for the probability of an alarm in any window of m steps: 5.146% (390, 7800) and 5.044% (1440, 28,800). This bound is unconditional; given the state at the start of the window it can fail badly (about 32% for the next step from a state just below the threshold). Measured: at most 0.18% (i.i.d.) and 0.40% (bold play).
* **The e-CUSUM bound fails without exchangeability (Proposition 3, proved).** A martingale-difference null stream that parks the statistic just below the threshold and then strikes has a window probability of at least about 1 / B = 11% in the limit, for every m and A. At full scale it passes the i.i.d. bound on day 17 (390) and day 16 (1440) and reaches 6.16% (390) and 6.44% (1440) on day 20.
* **Delay.** At a proved 5% for every day (known baseline), the restarted SR detector's mean delay was 1.06 to 1.44 times the plain detector's (390-step days) and 1.02 to 1.14 times (1440), within the renewal bound of Proposition 2 in every cell; the e-CUSUM at its certified A was 1.30 to 1.83 and 1.24 to 1.66 times slower. The plain detector is 14% to 31% faster than a fresh start because it enters the change with the statistic built up under the null, the same accumulation that raises its later-day false alarm probability.
* **Theorem D (M4).** Restated in `docs/math.md` with (H↑) `sup_{T<t≤T+h} μ_t ≤ (1 + b) min_{n_τ<i≤T} μ_i` and (H↓) `inf_{T<t≤T+h} μ_t ≥ (1 - b) max_{n_τ<i≤T} μ_i` (h = m for the bound within m steps), plus a part 4 with no assumption on the conditional means: `P(alarm within m) ≤ δ + P(tolerance fails within m) + m / A`. The proof goes through unchanged except that a weighted average lies between the smallest and largest of its terms; the bet-weighted version is kept as a remark. Under GARCH(1,1) clustering the band needed per path has a median of 0.90 to 5.01; no path of any cell satisfied the tolerance with b = 0.25, and parts 1 to 3, which need it almost surely, never apply.

| GARCH(1,1), persistence 0.99 | 390 | 2.58 | 0.71 | 2.58 | 4.82 | 0 | 4.2% |
| GARCH(1,1), persistence 0.999 | 390 | 1.62 | 0.62 | 1.62 | 3.54 | 0 | 28.4% |

| log-normal SV, log-sd 0.15, half-life 390 | 390 | 0.54 | 0.37 | 0.58 | 1.07 | 32.7% | 87.3% |

No path of any cell satisfied the tolerance with b = 0.25. These are per-path bands. Parts 1 to 3 of Theorem D need the tolerance almost surely, which no band below 1 achieves under GARCH (in every GARCH cell 44% to 100% of the paths need b > 1), so they never apply to these models; the per-path bands are what part 4 charges through the probability that the tolerance fails, which is 1 at b = 0.25 in every cell. Since b must be below 1 on the decrease side, the two-sided theorem excludes GARCH clustering at these persistences; the theorem's main case is a constant conditional law (Corollary 6.5). With a known baseline (Theorem B) only the conditional mean against m0 matters, and the calibration window plays no role.

### Relation to the literature

Lai (1998) bounds `sup_k P_∞(k ≤ T < k + m)`; Theorem 2 gives this criterion for the e-CUSUM uniformly over exchangeable nulls, Theorem 1 gives it for the restarted detector with a known baseline over the martingale-difference null for windows aligned with days (and `(2m + κ) / A` otherwise), and the plain detector satisfies it only for k = 1. Pergamenchtchikov and Tartakovsky (2018) use a maximal local probability of a false alarm in a window of fixed length, with a known pre-change law; Theorem 1 bounds the corresponding hazard by m / A for every day. Mei (2008) shows that with composite (mixture) pre-change models the average run length can mislead; Theorem A holds here for every null law while the day-40 example and the referee's family show day-level probabilities far above 5%, and Corollary C is a rate statement of the kind Mei recommends. Shekhar and Ramdas (2024) start a confidence sequence at every time and declare a change when their intersection is empty; Theorem D uses one confidence sequence on a calibration window as the baseline of an e-detector, needs a change-free calibration window, and gives a finite-horizon bound and a long-run count. All four were checked by web search only (arxiv.org and the publishers' pages could not be opened from this machine); the theory note says which statements rest on abstracts or secondary sources.

### Reading

"5% per day" is true of the first day after each (re)calibration, and of the long-run average number of false alarms per day, but not of every day. For ordinary i.i.d. returns the later-day hazard of the plain detector levels off just below 5%, so the misreading is mild there; for a null stream that is calm and then ordinary, or that watches the detector, it is wrong by a factor up to 13 (65% on day 20) or by a few tenths of a point. If a per-day statement is wanted, restarting the statistics at every day boundary gives it, with a known baseline, for every null law of Theorem B at a delay cost of 2% to 14% for 1440-step days and 6% to 44% for 390-step days; the e-CUSUM gives a window bound that also holds for windows that are not aligned with days, but only for exchangeable nulls, and it is slower. `PeriodicVolatilityMonitor(period=m, baseline="known", tau=..., m0=...)` implements this in the streaming monitor without changing `VolatilityMonitor`. With an estimated baseline only the confidence-sequence version carries a per-day proof (δ + m / A for each day, not given the past, while the tolerance of Theorem D holds), and the default plug-in version carries none.

### Caveats

* The simulations and Theorems 1 and 2 are for a known baseline. With the confidence-sequence baseline, Corollary 1 of the theory note gives `δ + m / A` for each day of a segment, marginally (given the observed past the probability is bounded only by `P(bounds failed | past) + m / A`) and only while the tolerance of Theorem D holds to the end of that day; the plug-in baseline is not covered by any per-day statement (Proposition A.6 of `docs/theory_running_tau.md`).
* Theorem 2 needs fixed bets; the adaptive bet of `detectors.betting_edetector` breaks the time reversal. Its bounds are unconditional; given the past only Lemma 2 holds. Whether `log A + H(w)` in Theorem 2(b) can be removed for the average over bets is open.
* The pooled bold-play hazard over days 11 to 20 and the renewal comparison were chosen after seeing the results. The tolerance numbers for stochastic volatility use the filtration that contains the volatility path; with returns only the conditional mean is smoother and the band needed is smaller.
* Park and strike is a lower-bound construction; how close a martingale-difference stream can come to the restarted detector's 5% after day 1 is not known (bold play reaches 2.75%).

The alternatives are kept apart from the main package in `alternatives/<name>/`, each with its own README (problem, mathematics, implementation, methodology, limitations), results and tests. `alternatives/ALTERNATIVES.md` ranks them. The sections below summarise each one.

## Report part ALT1: two alternative prototypes

Scripts, tests, READMEs and full results are in `alternatives/quarticity_stream/` (A3) and `alternatives/preaveraging/` (A1). Every number below is copied from the `results/` folders of those prototypes. [SYNTHETIC] marks simulated data, [REAL] marks Binance spot one-minute bars (1 July to 31 December 2025).

## A3. Monitoring quarticity itself: the e-detector on `min(r^4, tau^4)`

**Question.** The main monitor bets on the truncated squared return. The same bets on the truncated fourth power `Q_t = min(r^4, tau^4)` target the truncated local quarticity of Bapat (2026). Is that valid, how does it compare on pure variance changes, does it see changes of shape (tails, vol of vol) that the variance stream cannot, and what do its alarms mean on real data?

**Method.** Two things had to be derived: the null mean `q0` (the model-free sample mean of `min(r^4, tau^4)` over the calibration window; the Gaussian shortcut `3 m0^2` is 2.7% too high at `c = 3` and 21% too high with the raw MAD) and the decrease bet range `lambda < 1 / (tau^4 / q0 - 1) = 0.037` for normal returns, against 0.124 for the variance stream. With those, the proofs of `docs/math.md` section 5 apply unchanged. Settings as in E4: `tau = 3 x scaled MAD` from a 2000-step calibration window, `A = 7800`, 300 paths. A theory function computes the mean shift and signal-to-noise ratio of each stream under any alternative density.

**Q1 Validity [SYNTHETIC].** No change, 20,000 steps. False alarm within 390 steps (bound 5%) and censored mean run length (bound 7800): Gaussian 1.7% / 9471 (up) and 0.0% / 9046 (down); jumps 1.7% / 9348 and 0.0% / 9334; Student t5 2.7% / 8858 and 0.0% / 8558. Both bounds hold in every cell, for both streams.

**Q2 Pure variance change [SYNTHETIC].** Median delay in steps, Gaussian returns (jumps in brackets):

| sd ratio | x 1.25 | x 1.5 | x 2 | x 0.8 | x 0.67 | x 0.5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| variance stream | 96 (92) | 38 (40) | 18 (18) | 153 (151) | 95 (99) | 68.5 (74) |
| quarticity stream | 87.5 (91) | 33 (37) | 13 (14) | 271 (299) | 201.5 (216) | 168 (189) |

**Q3 Shape changed, variance fixed [SYNTHETIC].** 20,000 steps after the change, `A = 400,000` (null false alarm within the horizon at most 5%), 200 paths. Share detected (median delay):

| Alternative | variance stream, up | variance stream, down | quarticity stream, up |
|---|---|---|---|
| Student t3 / t5 / t8 | 0% / 0% / 3% | 100% (650) / 96.5% (3937) / 57.5% (8448) | 6% / 71.5% (6461) / 75% (7626) |
| two-point mixture, d = 0.5 / 0.7 / 0.9 | 8% / 5% / 2% | 28% / 46% / 58% | 82.5% (4915) / 99.5% (2678) / 99% (1033) |
| slow SV, log-sd 0.3 / 0.5 | 100% (715) / 100% (496) | 100% (524) / 100% (271) | 100% (664) / 100% (442) |

**Q4 Real data [REAL].** `A = 28,800` (each side alarms at 2A), 1440-minute calibration, recalibration after each alarm, band 0.25. Alarms per day: variance monitor 0.69 (BTC) and 0.69 (DOGE); quarticity monitor 0.71 and 0.70. Share of quarticity alarms on the same UTC day as a variance alarm: 87% and 87%; within one hour: 62% and 60%. Median truncated variance in the next 24 hours over the baseline: 1.45 and 1.38 after up alarms, 0.59 and 0.66 after down alarms (control at random times: 1.00). The 34 to 35 quarticity alarms per coin that are more than four hours from any variance alarm are still followed by a move in the flagged direction 80% and 88% of the time. All monitors on both coins alarmed at 15:28 to 15:31 UTC on 10 October 2025, the crypto crash after the US tariff announcement (checked online, `results/q4_real_event_check.csv`). With the same variance tolerance (band 0.5625 on quarticity), the quarticity monitor alarms 20% less often and its decrease alarms are followed by lower variance 100% and 97% of the time.

**Reading.**
* Valid, as the theory says.
* On pure variance changes the quarticity stream is 1% to 28% *faster* for increases (the fourth power amplifies the shift more than it adds noise) and 1.8 to 2.6 times slower for decreases (the bet cap).
* It detects vol-of-vol changes at fixed variance that the variance stream cannot (82% to 99% against 2% to 8%), but it does *not* beat the variance stream on fat tails at `c = 3`: clipping at 3 sd removes most of a fat tail's fourth moment, while the extra mass near zero lowers the truncated variance, so a Student t registers on the variance stream as a volatility *decrease*. At `c = 5` the theory reverses the ranking. The clipping level decides which shape changes are visible.
* On real data the two monitors behave alike; no pure shape event was found in six months of two coins. A planned shape diagnostic (`q_ratio / var_ratio^2`) measured only the mechanics of a fixed `tau` and is reported as such.

**Caveats.** Shape detection needs thousands of steps (signal-to-noise 0.03 to 0.10 per step). A first version of Q3 with `A = 7800` was unreadable because the null itself alarms within 10,000 steps on half the paths; the fix is recorded in `docs/iterations/ALT1.md`.

## A1. Pre-averaging before MAD truncation: microstructure noise at one-second sampling

**Question.** Under the standard price-noise model, at what noise-to-signal ratio `gamma = omega / (sigma sqrt(delta))` does the plain truncated estimator break, for integrated quarticity and for the monitor's local variance, and does pre-averaging (Jacod, Li, Mykland, Podolskij and Vetter 2009) followed by truncation fix it? What happens to the monitor's false alarm rate under noise, with and without pre-averaging, given that pre-averaged returns overlap?

**Method [SYNTHETIC].** One-second returns, 23,400 per day, daily volatility 1%, log-OU stochastic volatility, optional 4 jumps per day of 50 per-second sd, noise sd `gamma` times the per-second return sd. Pre-averaging window `k = 60`, weight `min(x, 1 - x)`; the local pre-averaged variance `V_i = rbar_i^2 / (k psi2 delta)` has mean `sigma^2 + c` with `c = omega^2 psi1 / (psi2 k^2 delta)`, and the local quarticity is corrected as `Q_i = rbar_i^4 / (3 (k psi2 delta)^2) - 2 c V_i + c^2`, whose mean is `sigma^4`; `omega^2` is minus the first autocovariance of clipped raw returns. Truncation of `rbar` at `3 x scaled MAD` by clipping (the paper's rule) or dropping, each with its Gaussian survival factors. Monitors run at `A = steps per day / 0.05`.

**Q1 Integrated quarticity, mean ratio to the truth (relative RMSE) [SYNTHETIC].**

| gamma | 0 | 0.25 | 0.5 | 1 | 2 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| raw returns, MAD clip, no jumps | 0.99 (0.02) | 1.26 (0.26) | 2.23 (1.24) | 9.0 (8.1) | 81.4 (81.5) | 1138 (1155) |
| pre-averaged, MAD clip, no jumps | 0.99 (0.11) | 1.00 (0.11) | 1.00 (0.12) | 0.99 (0.10) | 0.99 (0.11) | 0.99 (0.11) |
| pre-averaged, MAD clip, no noise correction | 0.99 (0.11) | 1.00 (0.11) | 1.00 (0.12) | 1.00 (0.10) | 1.01 (0.12) | 1.10 (0.15) |
| pre-averaged, MAD clip, 4 jumps | 1.14 (0.22) | 1.15 (0.22) | 1.14 (0.20) | 1.17 (0.22) | 1.18 (0.25) | 1.15 (0.24) |
| pre-averaged, MAD drop, 4 jumps | 0.99 (0.12) | 1.00 (0.13) | 1.00 (0.11) | 1.01 (0.12) | 1.02 (0.12) | 0.99 (0.12) |
| pre-averaged, no truncation, 4 jumps | 33.4 (69) | 36.5 (68) | 27.0 (47) | 35.1 (63) | 39.3 (71) | 32.5 (52) |

The raw estimator follows `(1 + 2 gamma^2)^2` exactly: 10% bias at `gamma = 0.16`, a factor 2 at 0.45. Integrated variance follows `1 + 2 gamma^2` (10% at 0.22). The monitor's 300-second local variance on raw returns is inflated by the same `1 + 2 gamma^2` (1.51 at `gamma = 0.5`, 3.07 at 1), while the pre-averaged local variance has mean ratio 0.98 to 1.07 at every noise level but a typical error of 32% (overlapping) to 45% (blocks) against 6% for raw returns without noise.

**Q3 One-day false alarm rate of the monitor, increase side (bound 5%) [SYNTHETIC].**

| gamma | 0 | 0.5 | 1 | 2 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| raw returns (23,400 steps) | 5.0% | 8.5% | **18.0%** | **31.0%** | **41.5%** |
| overlapping pre-averaged, k = 60 | **100%** | **100%** | **100%** | **100%** | **100%** |
| non-overlapping blocks, k = 60 / 20 / 10 | 2.5% / 4.5% / 5.5% | 1.5% / 3.0% / 5.0% | 2.5% / 2.5% / 5.5% | 2.0% / 5.5% / 2.5% | 4.0% / 3.0% / 3.0% |

**Q4 Median detection delay in seconds, sd doubles at the start of the day [SYNTHETIC].** Raw returns 32, 43.5, 86.5, 449.5, 2907 at `gamma = 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4`; blocks with `k = 10`: 259, 269, 299, 359, 649; `k = 60`: 1319 to 1379 throughout. For a halving at `gamma = 4` the raw monitor detects on 70% of days (median 10,795 s); the `k = 10` blocks on 100% (3939 s).

**Reading.**
* Truncation alone does nothing against noise; the plain estimator is off by 26% at `gamma = 0.25` and useless by `gamma = 1`. Pre-averaging then truncation is unbiased at every noise level, at the cost of a relative RMSE of 0.11 instead of 0.02 when there is no noise. Switch it on when the estimated `gamma` exceeds about 0.15.
* After pre-averaging, clip must become drop: a clipped jump keeps `tau^4` in each of the `k - 1` windows it enters (+12% to +18% with 4 jumps per day, growing with `k`).
* Overlapping pre-averaged returns break the e-detector completely: the conditional-mean null fails because consecutive windows share `k - 2` returns. Blocks on disjoint prices restore it at every `k`.
* **The raw-return monitor also loses its guarantee under price noise** (8.5% at `gamma = 0.5`, 41.5% at 4). With price noise `E[r_t^2 | past] = sigma^2 delta + omega^2 + E[u_{t-1}^2 | past]`, so squared returns are positively autocorrelated and the conditional null fails. E4 of the main report saw 3.7% at `gamma = 0.5` only because it looked at 390 steps. The remark in `docs/math.md` 5.1 that the null allows any dependence should be qualified: only dependence that keeps the *conditional* moment on the null side.
* The practical monitor at one second is the `k = 10` block monitor: valid at every noise level, 8 times slower than raw returns without noise, faster than them (and valid, which they are not) from `gamma` of about 2.

**Caveats.** Constant volatility in Q3 and Q4 (so the noise effect is isolated); i.i.d. Gaussian noise, which real noise is not (Hansen and Lunde 2006); the fourth-moment correction assumes local Gaussianity of the pre-averaged return; no real one-second data was available in this environment.

## A1 follow-up (B69). Noise and jumps together, the published benchmark, and the block monitor's guarantee

**Question.** When microstructure noise and jumps are present at the same time, how does pre-averaging then MAD truncation compare with the estimator built for exactly that case, the modulated bipower and multipower variation of Podolskij and Vetter (2009, *Bernoulli* 15(3), 634 to 658), for integrated quarticity and variance? And for the monitor: what exactly is the guarantee of the non-overlapping block version under price noise, and how should the block size `k` be chosen?

**Method [SYNTHETIC].** `alternatives/preaveraging/run_benchmark.py` (two processes, about 2 minutes). Q5: one-second returns, 23,400 per day, log-OU stochastic volatility, 200 paths per cell, noise ratio `gamma` in `{0, 0.5, 1, 2}` x jumps per day and size in `{none, 2 x 25 sd, 2 x 100 sd, 8 x 25 sd, 8 x 100 sd}` (25 per-second sd is 0.16% of the price). Estimators: raw MAD clip (Bapat 2026); pre-averaged (`k = 60`) MAD drop (ours) and MAD clip; modulated bipower (variance) and tripower (quarticity) variation with `K = 76`-step increments averaged over 152 blocks of 153 observations (`c1 = 0.5`, `c2 = 1`), noise-corrected through the exact block weights; pre-averaged bipower and tripower; pre-averaged without truncation. Q6: constant volatility, `gamma` in `{0.5, 1, 2, 4}`, blocks `k` in `{4, 6, 10, 14, 20, 30, 60}`, `A = (n / k) / 0.05`, sd `x 2`, `x 1.5` and no change, 200 paths per cell.

**Reference check.** Title, authors, journal, volume and pages of Podolskij and Vetter (2009) and the arXiv listing 0909.0827 were confirmed from search listings; the full text could not be fetched (arxiv.org, projecteuclid.org, repec.econ.au.dk and eldorado.tu-dortmund.de are blocked here). The block-average variance constants `nu1 = c1^2 (3 c2 - 4 c1) / (3 (c2 - c1)^2)` and `nu2 = 2 c1 / (c2 - c1)^2`, and the CLT standard error from the independent Gaussian block approximation, are therefore our own derivation, verified by simulation in the tests; no equation numbers are quoted.

**The negative finding, in one table. One-day false alarm rate of the monitor under price noise, bound 5%, 200 days per cell [SYNTHETIC].**

| monitor (steps per day, `A`) | side | gamma = 0 | 0.5 | 1 | 2 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| raw truncated returns (23,400, 468,000) | up | 5.0% | **8.5%** | **18.0%** | **31.0%** | **41.5%** |
| raw truncated returns | down | 7.5% | **9.0%** | **13.5%** | **29.0%** | **27.5%** |
| overlapping pre-averaged, k = 60 (23,341, 466,820) | up and down | **100%** | **100%** | **100%** | **100%** | **100%** |
| non-overlapping blocks, k = 60 (390, 7800) | up | 2.5% | 1.5% | 2.5% | 2.0% | 4.0% |
| non-overlapping blocks, k = 60 | down | 0.0% | 0.5% | 1.0% | 2.0% | 1.5% |
| non-overlapping blocks, k = 20 (1170, 23,400) | up | 4.5% | 3.0% | 2.5% | 5.5% | 3.0% |
| non-overlapping blocks, k = 20 | down | 3.0% | 5.0% | 1.0% | 3.5% | 2.5% |
| non-overlapping blocks, k = 10 (2340, 46,800) | up | 5.5% | 5.0% | 5.5% | 2.5% | 3.0% |
| non-overlapping blocks, k = 10 | down | 1.5% | 4.0% | 2.0% | 2.0% | 4.5% |
| non-overlapping blocks, k = 4 (5850, 117,000), Q6 | up | n/a | 4.5% | 4.5% | 3.5% | 4.5% |

Monte Carlo sd of each entry is about 1.5 points at a true 5%. The raw-return monitor's rate rises monotonically with `gamma` on both sides; the block monitors stay within the bound in all 58 cells (28 of Q6, 30 of Q3, with the four entries above 5% within 1.5 points of it).

**Why: the conditional null under MA(1) noise, and what blocks restore.** With observed prices `Y_j = X_j + u_j` (noise i.i.d., mean zero, variance `omega^2`, any distribution) the raw return is `r_t = Delta X_t + u_t - u_{t-1}` and, with `F_{t-1}` containing `Y_{t-1}`, `E[r_t^2 | F_{t-1}] = sigma^2 delta + omega^2 + E[u_{t-1}^2 | F_{t-1}]`. The last term has mean `omega^2` but is not constant (for Gaussian noise and the previous return alone, `E[r_t^2 | r_{t-1}] = sigma^2 delta + 2 omega^2 + rho_u^2 (r_{t-1}^2 - sigma^2 delta - 2 omega^2)` with `rho_u = gamma^2 / (1 + 2 gamma^2)`), so after a large squared return the conditional mean exceeds the baseline with no change in volatility: the null `E[Y_t | F_{t-1}] <= 1` of the e-detector fails, and so does the bound. The block monitor uses `Z_b = min(rbar_b^2, tau^2)` with `rbar_b` pre-averaged over the prices `Y_{bk}, ..., Y_{bk+k-1}`; the return between `Y_{bk+k-1}` and `Y_{(b+1)k}` is skipped, so block `b+1` shares no price with block `b`, its noise values are fresh, and given everything up to the end of block `b` it has the law of a pre-averaged return of a process started there. The independence is exact, not up to a boundary term (if adjacent blocks shared one price the shared noise value would give `Cov(rbar_b, rbar_{b+1}) = -omega^2 / k^2`, an `O(1/k)` relative dependence against the noise part `omega^2 / k`; skipping one return removes it). The null `H0: E[Z_{b+1} | G_b] <= m0`, with `m0` the calibration mean that includes the noise term `psi1 omega^2 / k`, then holds whenever the spot variance over block `b+1` is at most its calibration value and the noise and jump laws are unchanged, by monotonicity of `min(s^2 e^2, tau^2)` in `s`. The betting factor `1 + lambda (Z_{b+1} / m0 - 1)` with a predictable `lambda in [0, 1)` has conditional mean at most 1, so the Shiryaev-Roberts statistic over blocks is an e-detector with respect to the block filtration and Theorems A and B of `docs/math.md` apply with `m = floor(n / k)` blocks per day and `A = m / 0.05`. Nothing requires Gaussian blocks, so the guarantee holds for every `k >= 2`, which Q6 confirms down to `k = 4`. Full statement in `alternatives/preaveraging/README.md`, section 2.

**Q5 Integrated quarticity with noise and jumps, mean ratio to the truth (relative RMSE) [SYNTHETIC].**

| cell | raw, MAD clip | pre-averaged, MAD drop (ours) | modulated tripower (PV 2009) | pre-averaged tripower |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| no jumps, gamma = 0 / 1 / 2 | 0.99 (0.02) / 8.9 (8.0) / 81 (81) | 0.98 (0.11) / 0.98 (0.11) / 0.98 (0.11) | 1.00 (0.30) / 0.99 (0.33) / 1.00 (0.30) | 1.00 (0.13) / 1.00 (0.13) / 1.00 (0.12) |
| 2 x 25 sd, gamma = 0 / 1 | 0.99 (0.02) / 9.0 (8.1) | 0.99 (0.10) / 0.98 (0.11) | 1.12 (0.37) / 1.03 (0.34) | 1.06 (0.15) / 1.04 (0.16) |
| 2 x 100 sd, gamma = 0 / 1 | 0.99 (0.02) / 9.1 (8.2) | 0.99 (0.12) / 0.98 (0.11) | 1.63 (1.27) / 1.57 (1.73) | 1.45 (0.86) / 1.56 (1.63) |
| 8 x 25 sd, gamma = 0 / 1 | 1.00 (0.02) / 9.1 (8.2) | 1.02 (0.11) / 1.05 (0.12) | 1.27 (0.57) / 1.35 (0.65) | 1.21 (0.33) / 1.25 (0.34) |
| 8 x 100 sd, gamma = 0 / 1 / 2 | 1.00 (0.02) / 9.1 (8.1) / 81 (81) | 1.00 (0.11) / 1.01 (0.12) / 1.01 (0.12) | 4.9 (10) / 5.8 (14) / 4.5 (6.9) | 4.0 (7.8) / 3.6 (4.8) / 3.8 (5.2) |

Integrated variance: ours 0.99 to 1.02 (RMSE 0.05 to 0.06) in all 20 cells; modulated bipower 0.99 to 1.01 (0.13 to 0.14) without jumps, 1.05 with `2 x 25 sd`, 1.10 with `8 x 25 sd`, 1.16 to 1.20 with `2 x 100 sd`, 1.72 to 1.83 with `8 x 100 sd`. Coverage of the modulated bipower 95% CLT interval: 0.905 to 0.955 without jumps (half-width 26% of the truth), 0.905 to 0.97 with 25 sd or two 100 sd jumps, 0.57 to 0.62 with `8 x 100 sd`.

**Q6 Median detection delay in seconds for a doubling of the sd, blocks of size `k` [SYNTHETIC].**

| gamma | k = 4 | 6 | 10 | 14 | 20 | 30 | 60 | best observed | `k* = 6 gamma / 2` | rule `max(4, 4 gamma)` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | **127** | 179 | 269 | 370 | 479 | 749 | 1319 | 4 | 1.5 | 4 |
| 1 | **179** | 206 | 289 | 377 | 539 | 719 | 1439 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 2 | 405 | **332** | 354 | 419 | 539 | 764 | 1439 | 6 | 6 | 8 |
| 4 | 2131 | 1154 | 689 | **615** | 659 | 869 | 1439 | 14 | 12 | 16 |

For `x 1.5` the best observed `k` is 4, 4, 10, 20 against `k* = 6 gamma / 1.5` = 2, 4, 8, 16 (delays 299, 459, 839, 1539 s). The delay formula: after a sd change by `v` the block value has mean `(v^2 + rho_k) / (1 + rho_k)` with noise share `rho_k = 12 gamma^2 / k^2`, the bet grows by about `snr^2 / 2` per block with `snr = (v^2 - 1) / (sqrt(2) (v^2 + rho_k))`, so the delay in seconds is proportional to `k (v^2 + rho_k)^2`, minimised at `rho_k = v^2 / 3`, that is `k* = 6 gamma / v`. The curve is flat within 10% for `k` between `k* / 1.5` and `1.5 k*`, so the single rule `k = max(4, ceil(4 gamma))` (target `v = 1.5`, `gamma` estimated from `omega^2 = -mean(r_t r_{t-1})` over `mean(r_t^2) - 2 omega^2`) is within 10% of the best observed delay in all 8 cells.

**Reading.**
* The raw-return monitor's loss of validity under price noise is real, monotone in `gamma` and two-sided; it is not a Monte Carlo artefact (41.5% against 5%). It is the one claim of the main package that one-second data breaks. The fix is not pre-averaging as such (overlapping pre-averaged returns give 100% false alarms) but non-overlapping blocks, whose guarantee is exact for every `k >= 2`.
* Against the published noise-and-jump estimator, pre-averaging then MAD drop is unbiased over the whole grid and 2.5 to 3 times more precise without jumps; the modulated multipower estimators keep `|J|^{4/3}` per affected product at `n = 23,400`, a factor 4.5 to 5.8 in quarticity with eight 0.65% jumps, and its CLT interval then covers 60%. Noise and jumps do not interact for any estimator: pre-averaging handles one, truncation the other, and the two compose.
* The block size is a solved trade-off: `k* = 6 gamma / v`, in practice `k = max(4, 4 gamma)`. At `gamma <= 1` the smallest block (`k = 4`) is best and detects a doubling in 127 to 179 s, a factor 3 to 4 behind the raw monitor's 43.5 to 86.5 s, which is invalid there; the previously reported factor 8 came from `k = 10`.

**Needed changes outside ALT1's files.** `docs/math.md` 5.1 ("the null allows any dependence") and 5.6 should say that MA(1) price noise breaks the conditional null on raw returns and that the block monitor restores it; `ALTERNATIVES.md` A1 can record the benchmark outcome.

**Caveats.** All numbers are synthetic; i.i.d. Gaussian price noise (real noise is autocorrelated and heteroskedastic, Hansen and Lunde 2006); constant volatility in Q6; the delay formula ignores truncation; the modulated bipower constants and interval are our derivation, not the paper's printed ones; no one-second real data was available to estimate actual `gamma` values.
