## ALT2. Risk switch: does trading only on the monitor's alarms control risk better than volatility targeting?

Prototype folder: `alternatives/risk_switch/` (README with problem, mathematics, comparison with existing approaches, implementation and methodology; `RESULTS.md` with the full tables; `run_experiment.py`; synthetic tests). Script `alternatives/risk_switch/run_experiment.py`, tables rendered by `summarise.py` into `alternatives/risk_switch/results/summary_tables.md`.

**Question [REAL].** A long position is resized only when the monitor alarms, to `target volatility / (new regime's robust volatility)`, and held until the next alarm. Does this give better risk control than classic EWMA volatility targeting refreshed every minute, hour or day, after transaction costs? Benchmarks: buy and hold, EWMA targeting (Moreira and Muir 2017; Harvey et al. 2018, checked by web search), a daily-refreshed robust rolling estimate (same estimate, no change detection), and the same switch driven by the Gaussian likelihood-ratio monitor.

**Method.** Binance one-minute bars for BTC, ETH, XRP, SOL, DOGE (2024 and 2025) and Nifty 50 one-minute bars (April 2017 to October 2026). Exposure decided at the close of minute t applies to minute t + 1; cost = 5 bp (crypto) or 2.5 bp (Nifty) per unit of turnover, sensitivity 0 to 20 bp. Targets 40% (crypto) and 15% (Nifty) a year, exposure capped at 2. Every setting was chosen on 2024 crypto with a rule stated in advance (lowest tracking RMS among variants whose cost drag is at most 2% a year, mean over the five coins) and then frozen for 2025 crypto and for Nifty. Chosen: EWMA half-lives 3 days (minute and hour refresh) and 1 day (daily refresh); robust rolling 3-day window; switch with 5% false-alarm budget per session, band 0.75, no provisional trade; Gaussian switch with the same settings (over budget, flagged). Metrics: tracking RMS (root mean square of log(weekly realised vol / target)), realised vol, maximum drawdown, worst day, Sharpe with circular block bootstrap 95% intervals (10-day blocks, 2000 draws) and paired differences against daily EWMA, turnover, trades and cost drag.

**Results.** Out of sample, mean of the five coins in 2025 and Nifty 2017 to 2026, base costs.

| Rule | Crypto 2025: tracking RMS | max drawdown | worst day | trades / yr | cost drag | Nifty: tracking RMS | max drawdown | worst day | trades / yr | cost drag | Sharpe diff vs EWMA day, Nifty [95% CI] |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Buy and hold | | -61.0% | -16.9% | 0 | 0 | | -39.3% | -12.7% | 0 | 0 | +0.07 [-0.29, +0.44] |
| EWMA, minute | 0.192 | -40.3% | -13.5% | 525,600 | 1.6% | 0.256 | -28.9% | -4.9% | 92,613 | 0.6% | -0.01 [-0.09, +0.06] |
| EWMA, hour | 0.220 | -39.3% | -9.7% | 8,760 | 1.0% | 0.258 | -28.6% | -4.9% | 1,730 | 0.3% | +0.02 [-0.05, +0.09] |
| EWMA, day | 0.205 | -41.6% | -10.2% | 365 | 1.5% | 0.242 | -30.8% | -5.5% | 246 | 0.4% | reference |
| Robust rolling, day | 0.274 | -43.9% | -9.6% | 362 | 1.6% | 0.291 | -29.0% | -5.7% | 250 | 0.2% | +0.03 [-0.09, +0.14] |
| Switch, robust monitor | 0.271 | -40.9% | -10.6% | 93 | 1.6% | 0.402 | -28.1% | -6.3% | 12 | 0.1% | +0.10 [-0.07, +0.26] |
| Switch, Gaussian LR | 0.242 | -45.9% | -10.6% | 329 | 3.0% | 0.292 | -28.0% | -7.7% | 60 | 0.2% | -0.03 [-0.14, +0.08] |

Alarm rates of the frozen robust monitor: 93 a year per coin on crypto in 2025 (250 with band 0.25), 12 a year on Nifty; the Gaussian monitor 331 and 60. On the equal-weight crypto portfolio the switch's Sharpe difference against daily EWMA is -0.05 [-0.41, +0.32]. In 2020 on Nifty every targeting rule held realised volatility at 16% to 18% against 31% for buy and hold, with worst days of 4.4% to 5.4% against 12.7%.

**Reading.** The switch is a usable risk rule, not a better one. Its tails match EWMA targeting (drawdowns within two percentage points on crypto, smaller on Nifty) with a quarter of the trades on crypto and a twentieth on Nifty, and Sharpe ratios are indistinguishable everywhere. But it is a worse *volatility targeter*: tracking RMS 30% higher on crypto and 65% higher on Nifty, because exposure is frozen between alarms while volatility drifts, and each alarm-driven trade is four times the size of a daily EWMA adjustment, so crypto turnover (31 units a year) equals daily EWMA's despite fewer trades. The expected "matches with fewer trades" holds for trade counts, not for amounts traded. The one clear winner is the trigger: the robust e-detector beats the Gaussian likelihood-ratio monitor, which alarms three to five times as often, costs twice as much to follow and has worse tails on both markets.

**Caveats.** One out-of-sample crypto year (a weak one, so all Sharpe ratios are near zero) and one equity index; a single cost per unit of turnover, no financing or impact; the Nifty backtest is on the index, not futures; the cap of 2 on exposure matters for Nifty in 2026 (a steady decline where levered targeting drew down 18% to 25% against 16% for buy and hold). Full tables, by-coin and by-year breakdowns and the cost grid are in `alternatives/risk_switch/RESULTS.md`.

## Report part ALT3: a robust local plug-in estimator of integrated quarticity (A5)

Code, tests, README (mathematics, proofs, comparison with the literature) and full results are in `alternatives/robust_iq_estimator/`. Every number below is copied from its `results/` folder. [SYNTHETIC] marks simulated data or closed-form theory, [REAL] marks Binance spot one-minute bars (BTCUSDT and DOGEUSDT, 1 July to 31 December 2025, 184 UTC days each). Iteration notes: `docs/iterations/ALT3.md`. RK and RK-k below are this repository's version of the paper's kernel estimator (normalised weights, scaled MAD, c = 3, h = 30, without and with the kappa correction), not the formula as printed. PI-LU and PI-NN are proposals for discussion; where they do better, that is evidence from our simulation designs, not a claim to have improved the published estimator.

**Question.** Integrated quarticity (`IQ = int sigma^4`, the quantity that sets the width of every confidence interval for daily variance) is estimated in Bapat (2026) by clipping returns at `c x MAD` and averaging kernel-weighted local fourth powers. `docs/estimator_issues.md` raises four questions about it. What does the paper's idea (robust-scale truncation plus local smoothing) need in order to stay consistent when volatility moves during the day, how close can it come to the efficient asymptotic variance `8 int sigma^8`, can it be given a confidence interval, and how do such estimators behave on real minute data?

**Method.** Two changes of principle and one of detail. (1) Aggregate by **squaring a local variance** (the plug-in principle of Jacod and Rosenbaum 2013) instead of averaging local fourth powers: over blocks of k returns, `IQ_hat = sum over blocks of k delta (block mean of r^2 / delta)^2`, whose asymptotic variance is `8 (k + 3) / (k + 2) int sigma^8`. (2) Truncate against a **local** scale (median absolute deviation, then a truncated root mean square, over about three blocks) with either a fixed cut-off a = 3 or the growing cut-off `a_n = sqrt(2 log n)`, and **drop** truncated returns rather than clip them. (3) Remove the squaring and truncation biases with an **exact finite-sample correction**, computed from the cumulants of a clipped or dropped squared normal, so the estimator is unbiased under locally constant volatility for every block size. The same algebra gives `int sigma^8` and hence a 95% interval. Main proposal **PI-LU** (local scale, `a_n`, drop, `k = ceil(sqrt n)`). Second proposal **PI-NN** (added in iteration 3, after the real data): PI-LU with the scale raised to 1.4826 times the median of the six nearest absolute returns when that is larger, and blocks of `round(n^(1/4))`. Simulations: log-OU stochastic volatility from `avmonitor.simulate`, vol of vol 0.5 or 1 with a U-shaped intraday pattern, 0 or 4 jumps a day of three sizes, n = 390, 1440, 23,400, 500 days per cell, 15 estimators, true IQ known exactly.

**Q1 Efficiency [SYNTHETIC].** Constant volatility, n = 1440, 8000 days. AVAR in units of `int sigma^8` (closed form / simulated) and efficiency `8 / AVAR` (simulated AVAR where there is one):

| RQ | TPQ | MedRQ | MinRQ | RK-k (kernel, kappa-corrected) | PI-LU (k = 38) | PI-NN (k = 6) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10.67 / 10.81, 0.74 | 13.65 / 13.48, 0.59 | 14.24 (sim.), 0.56 | 18.50 (sim.), 0.43 | 8.19 (oracle cut-off) / 9.26, 0.86 | 8.20 / 8.46, 0.95 | 9.00 / 9.17, 0.87 |

The paper's averaged kernel is a truncated RQ with edge weights (`docs/math.md`, section 4), and truncation already lowers its variance from 10.67 to 8.19 with an oracle cut-off (efficiency 0.98, closed form) and to 9.26 with the estimated daily MAD (0.86, simulated). PI-LU's closed-form efficiency is 0.976. A jump clipped at a = 3 leaves 17.55 (plug-in) or 27.01 (fourth powers) times `sigma^4 delta` (simulation 17.56 and 27.02); a dropped jump leaves 0.003. At n = 390 each clipped jump is 4.5% to 6.9% of the day's IQ.

**Q2 Consistency [SYNTHETIC].** Strong stochastic volatility plus intraday pattern, no jumps (S5): relative bias at n = 390 / 1440 / 23,400 and slope of log RMSE on log n (minus 0.5 is the `sqrt(n)` rate):

| | RK (no kappa correction) | RK-k | PI-G3 (daily scale) | TRQ-M (Mancini) | MedRQ | PI-LU | PI-NN |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| bias | -0.209 / -0.159 / -0.144 | -0.179 / -0.128 / -0.112 | -0.069 / -0.061 / -0.055 | -0.038 / -0.028 / -0.024 | -0.017 / 0.005 / 0.002 | -0.002 / -0.001 / 0.000 | 0.008 / 0.006 / 0.001 |
| slope | -0.11 | -0.14 | -0.22 | -0.36 | -0.50 | -0.51 | -0.51 |

In S1 (vol of vol 0.5, no intraday pattern) RK is minus 4.2% to minus 4.7% at every n and RK-k minus 0.6% to minus 1.1%.

**Q3 Bandwidth [SYNTHETIC].** The cross-validation criterion as printed (eq. 17) picks the smallest bandwidth offered (h = 5) on 58% to 97% of days. Its expected value under constant volatility is 74.3, 77.2, 99.2, 142.8 at h = 5, 10, 20, 30 (minimum at h = 5 whatever the data). A corrected target picks the oracle spot bandwidth (median h = 50 to 150), but that oversmooths for the integrated quantity (kernel plug-in RMSE 0.250 at the corrected choice against 0.198 at h = 10, S5, n = 390). The block length of PI-LU matters little in smooth designs (default within 1% to 8% of the best k).

**Q4 Comparison and intervals [SYNTHETIC].** Relative RMSE at n = 390 (n = 1440 in brackets):

| | S1 no jumps | S2 small jumps | S3 medium jumps | S4 large jumps | S5 strong SV | S6 S5 + jumps |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ | 0.167 (0.091) | 0.631 (1.35) | 28.2 (102) | 3017 (12917) | 0.197 (0.111) | 31.2 (95.1) |
| TPQ | 0.189 (0.100) | 0.213 (0.125) | 0.630 (0.379) | 3.54 (2.99) | 0.239 (0.130) | 0.782 (0.383) |
| MedRQ | 0.186 (0.106) | 0.208 (0.111) | 0.471 (2.10) | 177 (93.4) | 0.236 (0.127) | 19.3 (1.19) |
| RK | 0.156 (0.091) | **0.156** (0.084) | 0.249 (0.091) | 0.312 (0.089) | 0.256 (0.184) | 0.198 (0.154) |
| RK-k | 0.156 (0.082) | 0.170 (0.091) | 0.280 (0.106) | 0.350 (0.107) | 0.236 (0.160) | 0.197 (0.134) |
| PI-G3 | 0.149 (0.078) | 0.158 (0.082) | 0.222 (0.090) | 0.261 (0.091) | 0.178 (0.109) | **0.191** (0.106) |

Bold marks the lowest of the 15 estimators in a jump cell. PI-LU is lowest in 6 of the 8 jump cells; in S2 and S6 at n = 390 the kernel and PI-G3 are slightly better, because their downward truncation bias offsets the upward jump bias (at n = 23,400 in S6 they are biased by minus 5% to minus 14%). PI-LU is best or within 0.01 of the best in 11 of the 12 cells at n = 390 and 1440. Its 95% interval covers the true IQ 92.6% to 97.2% of the time in all 18 cells (simulation standard error about 1%).

**Q5 Real data [REAL].** Median over days of each estimator's ratio to MedRQ of the same day, and rank correlation with MedRQ. The true IQ is unknown, so these are ratios between estimators, not errors:

| | RK | RK-k | PI-G3 | TRQ-M | PI-L3 | PI-LU | KPI-L3 | PI-NN | MinRQ | TPQ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BTC | 0.33 | 0.35 | 0.38 | 0.63 | 0.70 | 0.66 | 0.72 | **0.95** | 1.03 | 0.99 |
| DOGE | 0.42 | 0.44 | 0.46 | 0.66 | 0.71 | 0.69 | 0.73 | **0.96** | 1.05 | 1.03 |
| Spearman, BTC / DOGE | 0.865 / 0.814 | 0.865 / 0.814 | 0.879 / 0.837 | 0.927 / 0.890 | 0.939 / 0.908 | 0.931 / 0.888 | 0.941 / 0.911 | **0.975 / 0.965** | 0.995 / 0.994 | 0.987 / 0.987 |

**Q6 Bursts or jumps [REAL + SYNTHETIC].** Locally standardised one-minute returns: 65% (BTC) and 44% (DOGE) of returns beyond `sqrt(2 log n)` have a neighbour beyond 2 sd, against a chance level of 8.9% (`1 - 0.9545^2`) for independent Gaussian returns, and the lag-1 autocorrelation of capped squared returns is 0.114 and 0.099. A model with isolated jumps on slowly varying volatility gives 0 of 16 (1.4 expected by chance) and minus 0.008. That many apparent jumps are short bursts of volatility is documented for equities and currencies by Christensen, Oomen and Podolskij (2014, *Journal of Financial Economics*) and Bajgrowicz, Scaillet and Treccani (2016, *Management Science*); what is examined here is the consequence for truncated IQ estimators. A two-factor volatility model with a fast factor (sd 0.75 in log variance, half-life 3 minutes), picked from a 3 by 3 grid on these diagnostics, gives 41% and 0.120 and reproduces the real ratios (PI-LU / MedRQ 0.68 against 0.66 to 0.69; PI-NN 0.95 against 0.95 to 0.96; 1-minute over 5-minute MedRQ 1.41 against 1.33 to 1.45). In that model, median relative error and RMSE at n = 390 / 1440 / 23,400:

| | RK | PI-LU | TRQ-M | MedRQ | TPQ | PI-NN |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| median error, no jumps | -0.58 / -0.59 / -0.57 | -0.49 / -0.47 / -0.26 | -0.39 / -0.35 / -0.31 | -0.40 / -0.20 / -0.02 | -0.40 / -0.20 / -0.02 | -0.36 / -0.23 / -0.04 |
| RMSE, no jumps | 0.59 / 0.59 / 0.59 | 0.49 / 0.46 / 0.27 | 0.41 / 0.37 / 0.33 | 0.42 / 0.29 / 0.08 | 0.42 / 0.28 / 0.08 | **0.39 / 0.28 / 0.07** |
| RMSE, 4 jumps a day | 0.54 / 0.56 / 0.58 | 0.48 / 0.44 / 0.27 | **0.35** / 0.33 / 0.32 | 0.89 / 1.63 / 1.28 | 0.43 / 0.51 / 0.17 | 0.36 / **0.26 / 0.07** |

**Reading.**
* Under constant volatility, squaring a local variance gives efficiency 0.95 (simulated; 0.976 in closed form). That is a large gain over untruncated RQ (0.74) and the nearest-neighbour and multipower estimators (0.43 to 0.59), and a modest one over the paper's kernel with the kappa correction (0.86 simulated), which truncation already makes fairly efficient; its oracle version (0.98) is as efficient as PI-LU. The exact correction makes the plug-in unbiased at every n (without it PI-LU is 9.2% too high at n = 390).
* With a fixed c and one daily MAD, the kernel estimator converges to `kappa_4(c)` times IQ under constant volatility (minus 3.6% with the scaled MAD, minus 29.5% with the raw MAD), which the kappa correction removes. When volatility moves within the day, the corrected estimator keeps a bias that does not shrink with n: about minus 1% in the moderate design S1 and minus 11% at n = 23,400 in the strong design S5, where its RMSE falls like `n^-0.14`. This setting is outside the conditions of the paper's Theorem 1, which assumes a threshold that shrinks more slowly than the returns. A local scale removes the remaining bias for every truncation rule, and the growing cut-off with dropping (PI-LU) also removes jumps without a residual.
* The cross-validation choice as printed is driven by the criterion's scale term, and even a corrected criterion answers a different question for an integrated quantity: the IQ estimator wants less smoothing than the spot estimator.
* On real data the local estimators agree with MedRQ and MinRQ far better than those with one daily MAD threshold (RK is 0.33 to 0.42 times MedRQ, that is 2.4 to 3.0 times lower), but only PI-NN closes the gap. A possible explanation: large one-minute crypto returns come in bursts of a few minutes, which under the model are part of volatility. If the calibrated burst model is right, every estimator that truncates against a scale measured over hours is biased down by about 35% to 59% at one minute (31% to 56% with jumps); for our version of the kernel the figure is 56% to 59% at every n. The nearest-neighbour fourth-power estimators keep bursts but break with jumps. PI-NN combines both properties and has the lowest RMSE among the robust estimators in five of the six model cells (nearly tied with TPQ at n = 1440 without jumps; TRQ-M slightly lower at n = 390 with jumps).
* Practical suggestion: compute the clustering diagnostic first. Isolated large returns: PI-LU. Clustered ones: PI-NN, and agreement with a 5-minute estimate is no evidence of accuracy (in the model the 5-minute MedRQ is 0.57 of the true IQ at the median).

**Caveats.** PI-NN was designed after seeing the real data, with settings chosen in exploratory runs (other seeds), so its numbers are not strictly out of sample; it is worse than PI-LU with isolated jumps at small n (S3, n = 390: 0.320 against 0.179) and its `int sigma^8` estimate is not robust. The burst reading is a model fit, not a proof: clustered small jumps or microstructure effects could leave similar signatures, and the daily-scale estimators fit the real data less well (RK 0.53 in the model, 0.33 to 0.42 real). The two papers on bursts were read from their abstracts only. No central limit theorem is proved for the feasible estimators; coverage is numerical evidence. One venue, two coins, six months, no microstructure noise in the simulations.

## ALT4. Can the recipe detect a change in the correlation between two assets, without mistaking a volatility change for it?

Prototype in `alternatives/correlation_monitor/` (README with the formulation and proofs, `RESULTS.md` with every number, Q0 to Q4). Script `run_experiment.py`, results in `alternatives/correlation_monitor/results/`.

**Question.** Bapat (2026) names a multivariate extension as future work. The product of two assets' returns moves when their correlation changes, but also when the volatility of either asset changes or when one of them jumps. Is there a bounded statistic whose conditional mean moves with the correlation only, so that the e-detector of section 5 of `docs/math.md` applies unchanged?

**Method.** Two candidates. (i) The truncated product of standardised returns, `clip(r1 / s1, -c, c) clip(r2 / s2, -c, c)`, bounded in [-c^2, c^2] (the literal "truncated covariance"). (ii) The sign concordance `sign(r1) sign(r2)`, bounded in [-1, 1], with mean `(2 / pi) arcsin(rho)` for any elliptical pair, and invariant to any positive predictable rescaling of either asset (a two-line proof in the README). Both run in the Shiryaev-Roberts betting e-detector with an additive null band, each side at `2A`, so Theorems A and B hold verbatim. Benchmarks: a bivariate Gaussian likelihood ratio e-detector and a Page CUSUM on the raw product tuned to 5% per day under Gaussian pairs.

**Results [SYNTHETIC]** (2000 paths per row, A = 7800, 2000-step calibration, band 0). Share of paths with a false alarm within one day (bound 5%) and within five days (bound 25%):

| Scenario (correlation 0.3 throughout) | sign | product c3 | Gaussian LR | naive CUSUM |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gaussian | 2.9% / 23.0% | 0.0% / 11.3% | 5.0% / 32.0% | 3.2% / 18.4% |
| Student t4 | 2.4% / 23.1% | 0.2% / 15.7% | 79.8% / 100% | 96.2% / 100% |
| Jumps (0.5% per step, 8 sd) | 3.1% / 24.1% | 0.0% / 12.4% | 57.0% / 98.3% | 22.4% / 74.0% |
| Volatility of asset 1 doubles at step 500 | 2.6% / 23.6% | 0.0% / 98.3% (all "up") | 5.1% / 99.9% (97% "down") | 3.8% / 100% |
| Volatility of asset 1 halves at step 500 | 3.1% / 23.8% | 0.0% / 100% (all "down") | 4.6% / 79.6% | 2.7% / 48.2% |
| GARCH(1,1) clustering in each asset (alpha 0.05, beta 0.94), correlation fixed | 2.9% / 23.9% | 2.1% / 63.6% | 25.4% / 83.7% | 33.3% / 87.2% |

Median delay for a correlation change from 0.3 to 0.6 at step 500 (1000 paths): sign 174 steps, product c3 246, product c2 158, Gaussian LR 74 (but 70% to 100% false alarms before the change under t4 or jumps), naive CUSUM 125. For 0.5 to 0.9: sign 65, product c3 194, Gaussian LR 20. A growth-rate calculation predicts these delays within 25% and shows why the product is slow: its bound of 9 caps the admissible bet at 0.11, less than half the growth-optimal bet.

**Results [REAL]** (Binance 5-minute bars, 2024 to 2025, A = 5760 for 5% per day, calibration 5 days, band 0.1). The sign monitor raises 23 to 24 alarms per pair in two years. All 31 increase alarms are followed by a higher Pearson correlation over the next 5 days than in the calibration window (47% to 49% at random times), and 75% to 92% of the decrease alarms by a lower one. Increase alarms follow a negative 24-hour BTC return in 80% of cases and a bottom-decile return in 36% to 50% (10% by construction). The product monitor's decrease alarms coincide with drops in BTC volatility (median after / before ratio 0.83, against 0.99 at random times), the confusion predicted by the simulation; the Gaussian LR raises 4 to 5 times more alarms, 78% to 88% of them "down" and close to chance. At one minute the Epps effect (Pearson 0.02 to 0.06 lower than at 30 minutes) triples the number of "down" alarms, so 5-minute bars are used.

**Basket of four assets [SYNTHETIC and REAL].** The average pairwise sign concordance of k assets is bounded in [-1/(k-1), 1], so one e-detector at level A covers the whole basket with the same guarantee. Against the union of six pairwise monitors at level 6A it is twice as fast for a basket-wide change (72 against 132 steps for all correlations 0.3 to 0.6) and five times slower for a change confined to one pair (451 against 91), and it keeps its bound under t4 and volatility changes (19% to 24% per 5 days against 25%). On BTC, ETH, SOL and DOGE (raw 5-minute returns, band 0.1) it raises 31 alarms in two years; 93% of increase and 94% of decrease alarms are confirmed over the next 5 days (48% at random), and 8 of the 15 increase alarms follow a bottom-decile 24-hour BTC return.

**Reading.** The sign statistic turns the volatility monitor into a correlation monitor with the same guarantee, with no scale estimate and no truncation needed, and it is the only detector tested that a pure volatility change cannot trigger. It pays for this with a delay 2 to 3 times that of the Gaussian-optimal detector on clean Gaussian data, and is about as fast as the truncated product at c = 3, whose bets are throttled by Bapat's truncation bound.

**Caveats.** Plug-in baseline (a band of 0.05 to 0.1 or the confidence-sequence baseline of section 6 is needed; with band 0 the 5-day false alarm rate is 23% against a bound of 25%). The 5-day confirmation on real data can partly reflect mean reversion of the rolling correlation. The basket statistic dilutes a change confined to one pair; weighted variants and a forecast-relative null were not built.

## ALT5. Two-sample betting: can the monitor compare the recent window with the calibration window without estimating a baseline?

Code, tests, README (formulation, proof, comparison with the literature) and full results are in `alternatives/two_sample_betting/`. Every number below is copied from its `results/` folder. [SYNTHETIC] marks simulated data, [REAL] marks Binance spot one-minute bars (BTCUSDT and ETHUSDT, 1 July to 31 December 2025, 184 days each). Iteration notes: `docs/iterations/ALT5.md`.

**Question.** The main monitor bets that the mean of the truncated squared return equals a baseline `m0` estimated from the calibration window; its guarantee is proved for a known `m0`. Alternative A4 asks for a sequential two-sample test by betting that detects any change in the law of the returns, with nothing estimated. Is it exactly valid, how much speed does it give up on variance changes, what does it see that a variance monitor cannot, and what does it flag on real data?

**Method.** Each new return is ranked among all earlier returns of the segment (calibration window plus monitored returns, a growing reference), giving a smoothed conformal p-value. Under exchangeability these p-values are exactly i.i.d. uniform (Vovk, Nouretdinov and Gammerman 2003), so any bet `1 + lam (w(p) - b E_U|w|)` with a predictable witness `w` of mean 0 under the uniform law is fair, and the Shiryaev-Roberts mixture of such bets is an e-detector with the guarantees of `docs/math.md` 5.4 (average run length at least `A`, false alarm within `m` steps at most `m / A`), in the filtration of the p-values. The null band `b` allows the density of each p-value to be within `1 +- b` of uniform. Three bettor families: scale up and scale down bets on the Gaussianised truncated score `min(z^2, 9) / kappa2` of the p-value (the main monitor's statistic, but with null mean exactly 1), and histogram learners that estimate the density ratio of new to reference p-values (the rank-space analogue of a kernel two-sample witness, Shekhar and Ramdas 2024). Weights 0.25, 0.25 and 0.5, frozen from a pilot on development seeds. Truncation does not matter for ranks (monotone invariance, ties handled exactly) except to bound the Gaussianised decrease bet. Volatility clustering breaks exchangeability, as it breaks the main monitor's null. `A = 28,800` everywhere (5% per 1440-step day).

**Validity with no change [SYNTHETIC].** 1000 paths per law; share with a false alarm within 1 day (bound 5%) and 7 days (bound 35%), one-day calibration window, and within 1 day with a two-hour window:

| Detector | Gaussian, 1 d / 7 d | Student t4, 1 d / 7 d | Jumps, 1 d / 7 d | Two-hour window, 1 d (three laws) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| main monitor, plug-in, band 0 | 5.4% / **57.0%** | 6.0% / **52.5%** | 4.6% / **51.4%** | **42.0% to 45.7%** |
| rank detector, omnibus, b 0 | 2.4% / 22.6% | 3.1% / 24.2% | 2.4% / 23.0% | 2.2% to 3.5% |
| rank detector, fixed reference (240 / 1440 steps) | 90.4% / 100% and 21.2% / 98.4% (Gaussian, 500 paths) | | | |

The plug-in baseline's error acts as a constant drift that the bets find within days; ranking against the calibration window only (quantile bins learned once) fails the same way, because the p-values then share one reference and are dependent. With the growing reference every rate is below its bound at 1, 7 and 14 days. The repo's proved variant (`baseline="cs"`) is valid but conservative: 0.0% per day and 0.1% per week.

**Power [SYNTHETIC].** Change at monitored step 500, 400 paths, median delay in steps [share detected within 4000 steps when below 95%]:

| Change | main, plug-in, band 0 | main, confidence-sequence baseline | rank, scale bets only | rank, omnibus |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| sd x1.25 | 127 | 348 | 136 | 152 |
| sd x0.8 | 211 | 400 | 222 | 237 |
| Gaussian to t4, same variance | 1203 | 2251 [10%] | 1404 [86%] | **417** |
| jumps 0.2% to 1% per step, same variance | **361** | 1129.5 [92%] | 418 | 399 |
| jumps 0.2% to 0.5% per step, same variance | **1393** [88%] | not run | 1698 [57%] | 1688 [54%] |

The signed score (rank of `u` rather than `|u|`) alone detects a pure skew change (809 steps, 99%); for every `|u|`-based detector the law of the statistic does not change there. Truncating the rank score at 3 sd moves delays by at most about 6%. With a 120-step reference the rank detector stays valid (at most 0.8% false alarms before the change, bound 1.7%) and is 17% to 52% slower; the plug-in monitor with the same window has 11.5% to 14.0%. Under GARCH(1,1) clustering both designs alarm on most days (band 0.25, persistence 0.99: main 67.0%, rank 53.0%).

**Real data [REAL].** Returns divided by `intraday_scale`, one-day calibration, recalibration after each alarm. At band 0.25 the main monitor raises 127 (BTC) and 122 (ETH) alarms, the rank detector 123 and 114; 50% and 61% of the rank alarms are matched by a main-monitor alarm within an hour (chance 5.7%). Each monitor is calibrating about two thirds of the time, and 44 of the 61 unmatched BTC rank alarms (40 of 45 for ETH) fell while the main monitor was calibrating. While the main monitor was watching, the rank detector alone raised 17 BTC and 5 ETH alarms. The BTC ones are shape changes at constant scale: robust scale ratio 0.994, scale-free shape distance 0.131 against 0.076 at random times, and a learned density ratio of 0.32 for the largest 0.2% of moves and about 1.5 for the smallest ones, with more zero returns (5.0% against 3.8% in the reference). Dropping zero returns halves the group to 8, so part of it is a change in price stickiness rather than volatility. The main monitor alone raised 32 alarms per coin while the rank detector watched, all volatility decreases (truncated variance ratio 0.50 and 0.52). With a 120-minute reference the rank detector monitors 88% to 91% of the time.

**Reading.**
* The rank detector has the strongest guarantee of the designs tested: exact for any return law, any reference length and any horizon. The plug-in main monitor holds its bound for a day but not for a week (51% to 57% against 35%), which matters for every deployment that does not recalibrate daily.
* On variance changes it costs 4% to 7% in delay with scale bets alone and 11% to 19% with the full mixture; against the proved confidence-sequence variant it is 1.7 to 2.8 times faster. It is 2.9 times faster than the plug-in monitor for a tail change at fixed variance, which the variance monitors barely see. A change of jump intensity at fixed total variance is a negative result: the variance monitor is faster, because the diffusive variance falls.
* On BTC and ETH the two designs mostly agree; the rank detector adds a few shape alarms and misses some decreases at this band. Its practical gain is the short reference, which the plug-in design cannot use.

**Caveats.** Exchangeability fails on real one-minute returns (clustering), so real alarms are descriptive, not tested discoveries; ranks relative to a volatility forecast are the natural next step and were not built. The bands of the two designs are not on the same scale, so the real-data comparison is between two settings, not two designs in general. The rank detector gives no direction or size for shape alarms beyond the density ratio. About 80 microseconds per step in pure Python against about 10 for the main monitor (`results/t_timing.csv`). The conjecture that the Gaussianised score is asymptotically as efficient as the main monitor under Gaussian data is untested. One venue, two coins, six months.

## ALT6. Sequential fixed-accuracy estimation: how many minutes until the volatility level is known to plus or minus d?

Code, tests, README (formulation, proofs, comparison with the literature) and full results are in `alternatives/sequential_estimation/`. Every number below is copied from its `results/` folder. [SYNTHETIC] marks simulated data, [REAL] marks Binance spot BTCUSDT one-minute bars (1 July to 31 December 2025). Iteration notes: `docs/iterations/ALT6.md`.

**Question.** The main monitor asks whether volatility has changed. A simpler question comes first: after a restart, how long must one watch before the current level is known to within plus or minus `d` with confidence `1 - α`, and can the stopping rule keep its promise for heavy-tailed returns, jumps and clustering? The benchmark is the oracle sample size `n* = z² CV² / d²` (relative accuracy; `CV²` is the squared coefficient of variation of the statistic, unknown in practice).

**Method.** All rules work on squared returns after a 30-return pilot, either raw or truncated at `τ = 3 ×` the pilot's scaled MAD (the main monitor's statistic, Bapat 2026). Classical rules: Chow and Robbins (1965) with Nadas' (1967) relative version (stop when the estimated `n*` is reached), Stein's (1945) two-stage rule, Robbins' (1959) minimum risk rule. Anytime-valid rules: confidence sequences for the mean of the bounded truncated statistic (empirical Bernstein and betting, after Waudby-Smith and Ramdas 2024), stopped as soon as their relative width reaches `d`; their coverage at the stop holds for any law and any stopping time (Theorem 1 of the README). Proposition 1 (a sequential Bahadur and Savage argument) shows that no rule can do this for the raw variance, so the target is the truncated variance `θ_τ`, with a map back to `σ²` under a stated shape. Laws: normal, t5, t3, normal with 1% jumps per minute, GARCH(1,1) with persistence 0.95 and 0.99; 1000 to 4000 paths per cell, fixed seeds. Real data: one window per start hour (4392 windows) of returns divided by the past-only intraday profile, and a stationary bootstrap (Politis and Romano 1994) of the 30 quietest days.

**Classical rules on raw and truncated squares [SYNTHETIC].** Relative accuracy, `α = 0.05`, 2000 paths; "coverage / E[N]/n*":

| law | CR-raw, d = 0.2 | CR-raw, d = 0.05 | CR-trunc, d = 0.2 | CR-trunc, d = 0.05 | CS-bet, d = 0.2 | CS-bet, d = 0.05 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| normal | 0.948 / 0.97 | 0.942 / 1.00 | 0.952 / 0.99 | 0.942 / 1.00 | 0.982 / 1.84 | 0.969 / 1.57 |
| t3 | **0.765** / N 2225 | **0.721** / N 126482 | 0.944 / 1.01 | 0.949 / 1.00 | 0.973 / 1.73 | 0.973 / 1.57 |
| jumps | **0.783** / 0.47 | 0.929 / 0.96 | 0.942 / 0.98 | 0.945 / 1.00 | 0.976 / 1.79 | 0.973 / 1.58 |

**The price of anytime validity [SYNTHETIC, closed form].** As `d → 0`, a confidence sequence stopped at width `2d` needs `2 log(2/α) / z²` times the oracle without the running intersection of its bounds (1.921 at `α = 0.05`, 2.215 at 0.10; coverage at the stop 0.993 and 0.986) and a Brownian first-passage constant with it (1.548 and 1.708). Simulated with intersection (normal returns, pilot 100): 1.702, 1.576, **1.545** at `d` = 0.1, 0.05, 0.025. The factor is the ratio of the squared Chernoff quantile to the squared normal quantile, so it is the price of an exponential tail bound in place of the central limit theorem, not of time-uniformity. Time-uniform bets cost 5.6 to 14.6 times the oracle.

**Volatility clustering [SYNTHETIC].** GARCH(1,1), `d = 0.1`, 1000 paths; "coverage of the stationary level / coverage of the average conditional truncated variance over the window used / E[N]" (long-run `n*` 5370 and 22979):

| procedure | persistence 0.95 | persistence 0.99 |
|---|---|---|
| CR-trunc | 0.514 / 0.956 / 783 | 0.317 / 0.948 / 769 |
| CR-trunc with batch means | 0.911 / 1.000 / 4992 | 0.917 / 1.000 / 18916 |
| CS-bet, running intersection | 0.455 / **0.713** / 774 | 0.279 / **0.682** / 666 |
| CS-bet, no intersection | 0.695 / 0.992 / 1726 | 0.427 / 0.986 / 1815 |

**Real data [REAL].** BTCUSDT, `α = 0.05`, median minutes until stop over 4392 hourly windows (range of the 24 hourly medians), including the 30-minute pilot; no coverage is claimed:

| target accuracy | CR-raw | CR-trunc | Stein-trunc | CS-bet, no intersection | CR-raw not stopped within the start hour |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d = 0.4 (about plus or minus 20% on volatility) | 66 (52 to 82) | **50** (46 to 52) | 55 (49 to 58) | 140 (131 to 149) | **58%** (42% to 69%), CR-trunc 27% |
| d = 0.2 (plus or minus 20% on variance) | 411 (350 to 485) | **220** (200 to 230) | 220 (196 to 229) | 505 (447 to 551) | 100%; 6.0% not stopped within 24 hours |

Stationary bootstrap of quiet days, `d = 0.2`: with i.i.d. resampling CR-trunc covers 0.949, CS-bet 0.979, CR-raw 0.919; with 30-minute blocks every procedure covers 0.70 to 0.82.

**Reading.**
* Truncation is what makes the classical rules usable: CR-trunc covers 0.936 to 0.964 at 0.96 to 1.01 times the oracle in all 16 law and accuracy cells, for any pilot from 10 to 100 returns. On raw squares the rule fails for t3 at every `d` (0.72 to 0.78, with N growing like `d^{-3}`) and for jumps (0.78), and Stein's rule is worse (down to 0.36). In absolute rather than relative accuracy even normal returns under-cover at `d = 0.2` (0.90, a skewness bias of the stopped mean), so accuracy should be stated relatively.
* The anytime-valid betting sequence is valid everywhere and costs a known factor: about 1.55 times the oracle at small `d`, 1.8 at `d = 0.2`; on BTC, 2.3 to 2.8 times the minutes of truncated Chow and Robbins.
* Under clustering the stationary level is out of reach within hours (every i.i.d. rule stops 7 to 47 times too early; batch means needs 2,000 to 19,000 returns). What the classical rule does cover is the window's average conditional truncated variance (0.948 to 0.966, martingale central limit theorem). The running intersection of the confidence sequence is invalid for that moving target; without it the sequence covers it at 0.986 to 1.000. On real data the intersected sequence stops suspiciously early (1.32 against 2.20 times the in-window `n*` proxy at `d = 0.2`), the same signature, so the figures without intersection are the ones to quote.
* The hour of day matters little: the truncated rules' hourly medians stay within 10% of the overall median, because relative accuracy depends on the shape of the truncated squares, not on the level.

**Caveats.** The guarantee is for the truncated variance; the map to `σ²` is exact only under the assumed shape (2.5% coverage for t3 under a normal shape). The classical rules are asymptotic. Under clustering only the window average is covered, never the stationary level. The bets of the betting sequence are tuned for the rule without intersection (about 5% left in the intersected limit) and were not re-tuned; the pilot's returns are not used by the sequence. Deseasonalisation removes the intraday pattern but not quiet weekends, which cause most of the windows that never stop. One coin, one venue, six months.

---

## Limitations and further research

The limitations of all results above are collected in `docs/limitations.md`. The main open directions are: a guarantee that covers persistent volatility clustering without giving up power against structural breaks (E10 shows the trade-off is real); removing the blind period after each alarm (E12, E7); monitoring many assets with a single error guarantee (E15); and noise-robust monitoring on tick data (ALT1).
